People don't write any practitioner and then leave no road for the ones they didn't think of."

"And if there isn't?"

"Then I'll write four very good pages about a road that isn't there," said Karis, "and they'll be four better pages than the regional registrar is used to being sent, and he'll still send them back." She picked the pencil up again. "Go to bed. You've read everything I've written tonight, and nothing in it was untrue, and I'm going to sit here for an hour and be angry with the fifth part."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

She found it on the second day, in the middle of the afternoon, and she came up the residence stair at a run.

Cael heard her before he saw her. Nobody on the bluff had ever heard Karis run; she walked everywhere at the same even pace, as though the distance between two places were a sum she had already done. But there were feet on the residence stair taking it two at a time, and a door banging on the floor below, and Brom's voice on the landing saying "What—" in the tone of a man flattening himself against a wall. Then she was in Cael's doorway with Bracken's transcription held against her chest in both arms and her hair come half out of its pins.

"Schedules," she said. "The third schedule. Not the fifth part at all. It's tucked into a schedule at the back, between the fee table and the rules for travelling surgeons, where nobody has read it in forty years because nobody has needed to."

Brom had come up behind her and stood in the passage, enormous and alarmed.

"Is somebody hurt?" he said.

"Somebody," said Karis, "has been very clever, a long time ago, and then forgotten." She came in, laid the transcription open across Cael's desk on top of his ledger, and put her finger on a line about halfway down a page so close-printed it looked grey. "Read it aloud. I want to hear it in somebody else's voice."

Cael read it aloud.

"Practitioners for whom no tier seeding is applicable shall be scheduled per the demonstration-exhibition provisions."

He stopped, and looked up.

"Keep going," said Karis. "Two paragraphs down. The provisions themselves."

He found it. "Demonstration performances are rated against the Standard for performance rating only."

Lira had arrived by then too, in her stocking feet with a boot in one hand, drawn by the noise. The four of them stood round the desk in the small room with the window open and the fountain going below, and looked at a page of grey type that had been waiting there, unread, for longer than any of them had been alive.

"It's a fossil," said Karis. She had got her breath back, and her voice had gone level again, the voice she used for findings. "Before the registry standardized its classifications, there was an older way of evaluating practitioners who didn't fit the tables: you put them on a floor and watched what they could do. Demonstration. The charter was written in that era, and it kept a door for those people. Then the registry tidied everything up, and every practitioner on the continent got a tier and a rank, and nobody needed the door any more. So nobody ever used it." She tapped the page. "But nobody ever struck it out, either. It sat here. Unrepealed and unfashionable and perfectly good, just like the assay clause sat in Greyvane's charter until somebody needed it."

"So a fighter who can't be seeded—" said Brom slowly.

"—can be fielded. The charter answers its own objection. It says where to put him. The host doesn't seed him into a bracket. The host schedules him, under the exhibition provisions, and the panel rates what he does against the Standard, for a performance rating and nothing else." She took her finger off the line. "There's my door held open. The registrar doesn't have to swallow anything. All he has to do is turn three pages."

Lira put her boot down on the floor, very carefully, as though it might go off.

"So he fights," she said.

"So he's scheduled," said Karis. "Under a provision forty years older than any of us. Which means somebody at the first meet has to read it, and work out how to run it, and find out what a demonstration performance is in this century." She closed the transcription. "That's their problem. I've just solved ours."

Cael asked her what a demonstration had looked like, in the years when it was still done.

"Nobody knows exactly. There's a paragraph in the provisions about the floor, and another about the panel, and a third about how the rating's to be entered, and none of it's been used in living memory." She pushed a pin back in, uselessly. "The panel watches. The practitioner does what he does. They write down how well he did it against the mark. That's all a demonstration ever was, I think: being looked at properly by people who had agreed beforehand what properly meant." She glanced at him. "It's not so different from your provision. It's just older, and nobody's angry about it yet."

Brom looked from her to the closed book and back.

"You ran," he said. "Up the stair."

"I know."

"I've never seen you run."

"I've never found a schedule before." She pushed her hair back into its pins, without much success. "Don't write it down."

Cael had already written it down. He kept that to himself.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On the third night the four pages lay on the long table in a row, each in its final hand, and Bracken checked them.

He did it standing, with his spectacles on the end of his nose and the three charter copies open in front of him, and he did not read the pages as arguments. He read them as a list of claims about where things were. Every time a page said sixth part he turned to the sixth part. Every time it said third schedule he turned to the third schedule and laid his finger on the line and read the line aloud, in a low voice, and then read the page's quotation of it, and then said "Yes," and moved on. When a page gave a year he asked Karis where the year came from, and she told him, and he went to the shelf and found the volume and checked it. He took an hour and three-quarters over four sheets of foolscap. He found no error.

"Good," he said, and took his spectacles off.

Pages one to three he passed in the end without a word changed: the clause on its own, its angry history, and the memorandum's sentences set beside the charter's until the gap between them showed. The last page was one paragraph long, and it was Bracken's.

He had asked for it. That was the only time in a year Cael had known him ask for anything. On the second night, while Karis was still fighting the fifth part, he had stood at the end of the table and said, "If there's to be a last page, I'd like to write it," and Karis had looked at him and handed him the pencil.

It said that the enrollment record was true, and had been certified so, without omission, as the charter required. It said that the house stood ready to comply with the charter's mandatory language in every particular. And it said that if the regional registrar should determine that a true enrollment record must be altered before it could be accepted, the house respectfully requested that instruction in writing, over the registrar's name.

Cael read it twice. Then he looked up.

"That last line's a trap," he said.

"It's a mirror," said Bracken. He was cleaning his spectacles on his cuff, and he did not stop. "A trap catches you moving. A mirror just stands there. Let him sign an order to make a true record false, if he likes. The mirror will keep his name on it for as long as there are people left to read it." He hooked the spectacles back over his ears. "He won't sign it. Nobody signs that."

"Then what will he do?"

"What any careful officer does with a rule he doesn't like and can't break." Bracken gathered the four pages, knocked their edges together on the table, and slid them into a clean folder. "He'll write a short note asking for guidance, and send it to somebody senior, and go home early with a clear conscience. Then it's somebody else's afternoon." He tied the folder's tape. "Mind you, I don't blame him. I'd do the same, in his chair."

"Would you?" said Karis.

Bracken considered it honestly, which was the most alarming thing about him.

"No," he said. "I'd have read the third schedule first. But I've had twelve years at this counter to get into bad habits." He put the folder under his arm. "The chancellor signs tomorrow evening. I'll take it up at the sixth bell. She's asked for the enrollee to be there."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Withrow's office was at the top of the old range, up a stair that turned twice, and it looked just as it had looked a year ago, which Cael found he had been relying on.

A long desk bare of everything but the work in hand. A wall of grey file cases, each labelled in the same hand. Above the cases, framed and glazed and hung at the height of a person's eyes, the house's own charter, the founding one, its ink gone brown, hung there not as an ornament but where she could point at it. One window looked down the bluff to the river. The lamp on the desk was already lit, and the folder with the four pages lay beside it, open.

"Sit," said Withrow. "I want a witness who isn't on my staff."

He sat in the chair across the desk from her while Bracken stood by the door. Withrow read the four pages through, slowly, at her own pace, initialling each margin where her initials already stood on an earlier draft. She read the fourth page twice, then put the pen down, laid the pages together, and folded her hands on top of them, and looked at him across them.

"When this seal goes down," she said, "the house stands behind you fighting this season, in front of everyone, start to finish. You should know why. I'll say it once, and then you need never wonder. A great many people this year are going to offer you their opinion of my reasons. Most of them will say ambition, and most of them will be about half right." Her face did not change. "I want this house at Norhold. I've wanted it since before you came up the road. Your enrollment helps, and I know it helps, and I'm not going to pretend to you or to anybody else that I don't know it."

Cael waited. He had learned that Withrow did not need encouraging.

"Now look at the sequence. It's the only part that matters." She lifted one finger from the stack. "First there was a house. I spent a good many years making it a house that does difficult things in writing, in front of witnesses, and gets them right." A second finger. "Then there were rules: their charter, written by their own board forty years ago, before you were born. Nobody here wrote a word of it." A third. "Then there were people who keep the rules as written. A registrar who signs true records because he can't bear to sign any other kind. A girl in a reading room who reads the whole of a thing, including the schedule between the fee table and the surgeons." She did not glance at Bracken by the door. "And last of all, there was you."

She let the fingers lie flat again.

"Take your line off that roster," she said, "and every other sheet in this folder reads exactly as it reads tonight. The clause would still be there. The record would still be true. The schedule would still be where Karis found it. That is why it will hold. A thing built round one person comes down when that person slips. A thing built straight stands whoever stumbles in it." She picked up the pen. "I learned that last term, with an Archmarshal sitting in my records hall for eleven days. I'd been told it before. I'd never been shown."

She signed. She signed in full, her whole name, slowly, and Bracken came forward from the door with the seal and the wax, and the house's mark went down beside her name.

"Bracken," she said.

"Chancellor."

"The morning courier, please. Not the noon one."

"The morning one," Bracken agreed, and took the folder, and went.

Cael sat in the chair with his hands on his knees and found he had nothing ready to say. He had expected, he realized, to be told he was valued, or to be told he was a risk, and he had readied himself for either. He had not readied himself to be told that he came last in the order of things, after a house and a set of rules and the people who kept them, and that this was the reason the thing would stand. It was not a flattering account of himself, and it had been given to his face. It was also, he thought, the safest place in the world to be standing: at the end of a line of other people's honest work, where nobody could pull him out without pulling all of it down.

He looked up at the framed charter above the file cases, the brown ink and the old seal, and Withrow saw him look.

"The house's," she said. "Somebody wrote that a long time ago, too, for reasons of their own." She did not smile. "I read it once a year. It still says what it says."

Withrow sat back in her chair. The lamp made a small bright room of the desk and left the file cases in shadow.

"Go and train," she said. "If their charter holds, you've a season starting in a little over three weeks. If it doesn't, you've a quarrel starting rather sooner, and I'd like you fit for that too." She took her spectacles off, which in Withrow was the same as a door opening. "Thank Karis for me. Don't let her refuse it. Tell her it's from the chancellor and she has no standing to decline."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The first of Ephram's sessions fell on the morning after the signing, at the second bell, with Rooke at the rail of the second training floor and nobody else in the room.

It was the floor time the sheet had asked for, and it was not what Cael had expected. He had thought Ephram would come at him with the second-year entry until one of them dropped. Instead Ephram spent the first half-hour doing nothing but walking: walking at him off the chalk, at every angle the floor allowed, at every speed from a stroll to a lunge, with the lath held low and never once thrown, while Cael stood and called the weight aloud as it came.

"Front," said Cael. "Front. Both. Front. Front. Both."

"Both," Ephram agreed, on the third. "You called that one before my back heel knew."

"I called it off your shoulders. They drop when you're bringing everything."

Ephram stopped walking.

"Do they?" He tried it, standing still, loading the front foot and then both feet, and watched his own shoulders in the long window's glass. "They do," he said, in a tone of real annoyance. "Nobody's ever told me that."

"Nobody else reads shoulders that early."

"Rooke does."

"I didn't say anything," said Rooke from the rail, without looking up from his board. "I've been waiting a year for somebody else to."

Ephram looked at the rail, and then at Cael, and for the first time since Cael had known him his face did something that was very nearly a laugh, quickly mastered.

"Then that's mine to fix," he said, "and the heel's yours. Fair trade. Again."

In the second half-hour they worked at speed. Cael beat the second weight four times in ten, waiting for the heel or, when the heel was too quick, for the dip of the shoulders that told him it was coming. He ate the plain entry three times. Once he ate nothing at all, because Ephram, now thinking about his shoulders, threw the entry so badly that it went a yard wide and both of them stood looking at the lath in reproach.

Rooke wrote on his board. At the end of the hour he turned it round so that they could both read it, which he had never done before.

Enrollee: heel, one in three, nearer two. Ephram: shoulders. Good trade.

He turned it back.

"Again on Fourth-day," he said. "Same hour. Bring the shoulders."

Then the silence began, and the house went on preparing for a season with its eyes turned very slightly toward the road.

The response had gone down the bluff on the morning courier of the Sixth-day. After that nothing came back up, and the regional registrar did not write. The memorandum's fourteen days went on running down on the calendar behind Bracken's counter, one day a morning, each crossed off in his small neat stroke. In its turn the fourteenth was crossed off like the rest, and nothing went back down the hill to meet it. The house had answered once, in four pages, and Bracken did not resubmit; a true record, he told Brom when Brom asked, did not get any truer for being sent twice. The coats at the ferry landing and the road's foot changed on the bell, two and two, and Karis's marbled book got a line a day, and every line was the line above it.

Nobody spoke to Cael about any of it. He put it together out of the things people were careful not to do.

Rooke did not post the first meet's bout targets. Every other week on the calendar board had its targets pinned beside it in Rooke's hand, and the first meet's week had a clean space the size of a sheet where they would go. Bracken's clerk opened a travel file for the delegation and wrote out its cover in full, every name and wagon and stable fee, and left the date line blank. The wagoner came up from the town to look at the axles and went down again without being told which morning to come back. And at the counter on the Fifth-day, when Cael brought the week's coursework, the teaching assistant took it, read the head of it, and laid it in the tray face down, square to the others, and said "Mm," and that was all, as it should have been.

Five people's seasons sat on one line of a roster, and the line was his. If it failed, Lira's first season at Iron would open at a table instead of on a floor, and Brom's first chance to be priced by strangers with it, and Karis's, and Ephram's. He could not stop doing the sum. It came to meals with him and sat in his mouth instead of food.

The floor, at least, did not wait for anybody. On the Fourth-day Ephram came to the second session with his shoulders held so still that he looked like a man carrying a full tray across a crowded room. He threw the second-year entry at Cael twenty times in an hour, and Cael beat the second weight twelve of them by the heel alone, because there was no longer any shoulder to read. On the ninth throw he ate the plain entry clean across the ribs and let it pass. On the fourteenth Ephram's shoulders dropped again from tiredness, and Cael called it aloud before the heel had moved, and Ephram muttered something at his own shoulders and went back to his chalk. Rooke's board, at the end, said only Better. Both. Cael read it upside down on his way to the water jug, and carried it back up to the residence with him like a coin in his pocket, and turned it over at supper when the sum came back.

Hesk's answer came up on the evening coach of the Third-day, the fourth day of the silence, and it was four lines long.

Cael took it from his pigeonhole in the cloister and read it standing there, under the lamp by the porter's lodge, with second-years going past him in both directions on their way to supper. He had stopped trying to wait until the stair with Hesk's letters. He had never once managed it.

A list is an honest thing if the man who keeps it is. Sounds like yours is. Mind your feet on strange floors, and pack wool; a hall is always colder than the man who booked it says. Glad about the handle. Every man should have one thing he's foolish about. — H.

He read it three times. Then he stood in the cloister holding it and laughed, once, out loud, so that a Current girl going by turned to see what was funny and found nothing she could see.

Pack wool. Two men now, in a fortnight, had told him to pack for the cold, one across a counter in front of a queue and one across the whole width of the country in a hand that grew larger every year. Neither knew the other existed. One of them could not know what he was saying and the other could not say what he knew. Cael did not put them together in his head, because there was nothing to put together; quarry towns were cold and grandfathers were careful. But he noticed that he had noticed, and he wrote that down before he slept, because noticing was the only part of it that was his.

The letter went behind the front board of the observation notebook with the other two that lived there: the folded note that had come in the pine case with the pen, on the eleventh of Sowing, and the sheet that had said Sixteen suits you. Three now, in the same hand. He sat with the notebook shut on all three before he put it away, and did not write in the Log what it cost him to have them there together, because some lines in a ledger were better left as a space.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On the sixth evening of the silence Lira found him on the wall behind the second quadrangle.

She did not sit down at once. She stood with her back to the valley and her hands in her coat and looked at him, the way she looked at an opponent's mark before a bout, measuring where he would be standing when she arrived.

"Who signed it?" she said.

"What?"

"The response. Who signed it?"

"The chancellor."

"Who wrote the last page?"

"Bracken."

"Who found the schedule? Who sat up three nights in a stone hall with the porter bringing her tea? Who certified the record, and sanded it, and put it in a wallet, and watched the courier take it?" She took one hand out of her coat and held it up, empty. "Who decided to put Halcenvane in a tournament in the first place, a year before you'd ever heard the word clause?"

He did not answer, because she was not asking.

"Every one of them chose," said Lira. "In ink. With their names. And you've been walking round this house for a week carrying all of it on your own back like they'd dropped it on you in the dark." She sat down on the stone beside him at last, hard, with her boots hanging over the drop. "It's an insult, if you want to know. To them. You're counting their choices as your debts."

"If it fails—"

"If it fails, we fight it. We've fought paper before, the four of us, at Greyvane, with less than this, and we won. And if we lose a week of the season doing it, every house on the circuit learns that Halcenvane doesn't lie down when somebody sends it a sheet of short-inked type." She shrugged. "Withrow could tell you to the half-point what that's worth in standings. Ask her. She'd like being asked."

Below them the ferry lamp came on, and two grey coats stood under it.

"Brom," said Lira, "has started eating your bread without asking. That's how worried he is. Karis wrote me a card." She took it out of her pocket and handed it to him, a folded square in Karis's small hand, three numbered lines.

1. It isn't his weight. 2. He'll carry it anyway. 3. Make him list who chose.

Under it, in heavy pencil, in a hand that could only be Brom's: Tell him the floor's still the floor.

"I followed most of it," said Lira. "I left out the floor. I didn't know what it meant."

"It means whatever happens with the paper, the oak's still there in the morning, and so are the frames, and so's Ephram's second weight."

"Oh." She considered that. "That's better than mine. Don't tell him."

He gave her back the card, and she put it away carefully, a thing she meant to keep.

"You rehearsed it," he said.

"Since the second day of drafting. You went quiet at supper that night, when Karis came in with her hair down." She stood and brushed off her coat. "Come and eat your own bread."

She went off along the wall toward the lit windows, and after a moment he followed her.

He was smiling when he opened the Log, and went on smiling while he wrote.

They have a procedure for me now. They watch for the quiet. They choose who'll say the thing, and one of them writes it down for her on a card, and somebody adds a line at the bottom in pencil, and she's sent out to say it where I'll be sitting. I've been handled. By three people. With a card.

I'm entering it on the wealth side of the ledger.

Chapter 5 — Advisory

[Quiet, purposeful narration; carry the earlier cost into the new campaign without recapping it]

The routing slip was the first thing the Archmarshal read, because it was the only thing in the bundle that nobody had meant him to read closely.

It was pinned to the top of the file with a brass pin, a narrow strip of the Compact's buff paper with a printed column of offices down its left side and a ruled space beside each for a clerk's initials. Received. Logged. Assessed. Referred for advisory. Against the first three stood three sets of initials he knew, the ordinary clerks of the registry floor below his. Against the fourth, in a narrow, sloping hand he did not know at all, stood two letters he could not place, and after them, written out in full, his own name and title.

Vastin held the slip to the window and looked at the two letters for some time.

His room was high in the Compact's house, up a stair that the builders had made too steep and the clerks had worn too smooth. Its one window gave on a court where a man in a porter's apron fed pigeons every morning at the same hour from the same paper bag. Vastin had come to regard the pigeons and the porter as the most reliable instrument in the building. The room held a table, two chairs, and four shelves of files that were his only in the sense that he was the officer who would be asked about them. It was a little after the second bell. His left hand, which had begun some years ago to dislike mornings, lay on the table beside the bundle and declined to be hurried.

He set the slip down, face up, where he could see it.

Then he did a thing he had done all his working life with a file that had come up from below: he read the defence before the charge.

The academy's response ran to four pages, in a clean clerk's hand, under the house's seal, signed by a chancellor whose name he had last seen at the foot of a great many documents in a records hall. The first page was a single line of a tournament charter and its citation, and nothing else at all. He looked at the white space under that line for longer than he looked at the line. Somebody had written sentences in that space and taken them out again. He could tell, because the space was too exact to be an accident; a person who had never put anything there would not have left it so cleanly empty.

The second page was the clause's history, and the third was as good an argument as he had read from a provincial house in some years. It cited a schedule he had not known existed; he went to his own shelf and turned to it, and it was there.

The fourth page was a paragraph. He read it twice.

He had seen perhaps five such paragraphs in forty years. It asked for nothing. It offered compliance and requested, if compliance should require a true record to be made false, that the instruction come in writing over a name. A document that asked for nothing was a document whose author had already counted every door out of the room and shut each one, gently, without locking it. He did not know whose paragraph it was. He thought he might guess. A registrar at the top of a bluff above a river had kept an index that his own counsel had wished to find fault with and had not, and he had written to that registrar privately afterward, in four sentences, because good work should be told it is good. This paragraph had the same bones.

Only then did he read the charge.

The regional registrar's memorandum was a single item on a list of five, three sentences long, and he could see the joint in it from across the room. Cannot be seeded. Cannot be fielded. Defective. A man who had been frightened by a name on a list had reached for the nearest pair of words that rhymed, and had soldered them. Then he had sent the result up the chain in the hope that somebody above him would agree that the solder was steel.

And the question it raised, put in the registry's usual form, which asked whether a practitioner with no classification might be fielded under the tournament's charter.

Vastin sat back.

He knew the enrollee. That was the plain fact of it, and he did not pretend otherwise to himself. He had sat four feet from the boy in a room twelve feet by fourteen, some months back, and put eleven questions to him, and left a twelfth where it lay. He had watched him on a failing frame. He had written a line in his own hand into the file the Compact kept on him, and signed it with his name entire. Classification error is unlikely. Continue observation. Anybody above him who read that file had read that line.

So of all the officers in this building, he was the one best placed to answer this question, and somebody had known it, and had written his name in full against the fourth line of a routing slip in a hand he did not know.

He turned the slip over. The back was blank.

There were two reasons to send a question to the officer who had looked closest. One was that you wanted the true answer and knew where it lived. The other was that you wanted a particular answer, and thought the officer who had looked closest might be persuaded to give it, and that his giving it would be worth more than anybody else's. A man could not always tell from a routing slip which of the two he was holding. He could tell, after forty years, that the people above him were not fools. Whoever had initialled the fourth line had known exactly what they were doing, whichever it was.

It did not change the answer. That was the one comfort of a question about a text: the text did not care who had asked.

He took a sheet of the Compact's paper and a pencil and wrote the advisory long first, the way he wrote everything he meant to keep short. He set out the clause and its citation. He set out the schedule and its provision. He noted that the enrollment had been adjudicated at Greyvane on the public record and renewed at Halcenvane before a delegation of the Compact, of which he had been the senior officer. He noted that the registrar's syllogism joined two terms which the charter kept apart. He noted, because it was true, that the academy's response was correct in every citation and that he had checked them himself.

It came to a page and a half. He read it through, and it was all accurate, and it was all unnecessary, and some of it was the sort of thing a man writes so that a reader will know how carefully he has looked.

He struck it through, one line from corner to corner, so that the words could still be read beneath, and on a clean sheet in ink he wrote what the question needed.

The clause says what it says. The enrollment is lawful on its face and adjudicated at public record. If the Compact wishes practitioners of this kind not to compete, it should write different rules — not misread the ones it has.

Three sentences. He read them once and they still meant what he meant, and he knew no better test. He signed them with his name entire.

What would it cost him? He made himself ask it, because a man who does not price his own advice ends by giving the expensive kind for nothing. And the honest answer was: nothing. The advisory recommended no action and took no side. It quoted only what anyone could buy at a stationer's, and its one refusal was to find words in a charter that the charter had never held. He had built a career on the principle that the text governed, and had held to it in rooms with far worse air in them than this one. He would not let it bend for one enrollee, in either direction. It cost him nothing, yet. He made a note of the yet in his head, where he kept such notes, and did not examine it.

He pinned the advisory to the file, put the struck draft in his own drawer, and took the bundle down the too-steep stair to the dispatch room himself, before the noon post closed. The dispatch clerk logged it and gave him a slip. He put the slip in his coat.

Then he waited for the questions, because there were always questions.

A registrar who had been answered against his memorandum would write within the week, wanting language to stand behind: a sentence he could quote back to the house so that the house would know it was the Compact and not the regional office that had given way. Or an office above would write, wanting to know why the Compact's evaluator had once again declined to hand it a difficulty. One or the other. Usually both. He had the answers to both in his drawer, beneath the struck page.

Neither came.

The ordinary silence after an advisory had a shape he knew as well as he knew the porter and his pigeons: an acknowledgment from the receiving office, a file marked closed somewhere below with a clerk's initials, a line in the weekly digest. He had read that silence ten thousand times. This was not it. The advisory was received. He knew it was received, because the dispatch slip in his coat said so. After that, nothing. No acknowledgment came back up the chain. The file did not reappear in the digest. The two letters on the fourth line of the routing slip were not on any other slip that crossed his table in the next nine days, and he looked.

On the tenth day, among the morning's papers, he found a printed meet card from a regional host, filed for information, routinely, as all such cards were filed. He read down it until he came to the fifth line of one house's block. Then he laid it on the table beside the routing slip, and sat with his left hand open on his knee, watching the porter in the court below feed his pigeons from the same paper bag.

The roster stood. Nobody had asked him anything. Nobody had answered him.

He noted the fact, and he did not yet allow himself to note what it meant. A question that stops coming to the officer best placed to answer it has not stopped being asked.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On the Fifth-day the answer came up the bluff, and it did not look like an answer at all. It looked like a timetable.

Bracken laid it on the records-hall counter at the third bell with no covering letter, because there had been none. It was the first meet's official card, printed by the host's office on thick cream stock in two columns, and it listed every delegation entered at the wool town in the order of their registration, with each house's competitors in a block beneath its name. Halcenvane's block was the ninth, and it ran five lines. The first four looked like any house's.

C. Cael, enrolled practitioner, unclassified — scheduled per demonstration-exhibition provisions.

Karis turned the card over, and looked at the back, which was blank, and turned it face up again.

"No letter," she said.

"No letter," said Bracken.

"No ruling. No withdrawal of the memorandum. No answer to the response." She went through the bundle it had come in, a sheaf of hall plans and floor times and a list of approved inns, and set each sheet aside. "Nothing at all. Not a word to us. Only the card."

"They've cut him down, too," said Lira, reading over her shoulder. "C. Cael. Where's the rest of the name?"

"The schedule office cut it to fit," said Karis. "Caelen Hesk-ward, 41-7843-V is the registry's. The host's printer had two inches of column and a deadline. So he took the initial and the name the house calls him, and that's the line." Her thumb rested on the line. "It's the first time any official paper has ever called him what we call him."

Cael found he had not thought of that, and that it was true.

Bracken said, "That is how careful institutions surrender. In the schedule." He took the card back from her and held it to the light from the high window, as though checking it for a watermark. "A ruling has to admit that somebody asked a question. A schedule just says Second-day, third bell, Hall Two, and everyone turns up. Nobody can appeal a timetable. Nobody ever thinks to."

"So we won," said Brom.

"So we were printed," said Bracken. "Which in my trade is better." He laid the card in a clean folder and wrote on the folder's spine in his small upright hand. "Somebody upstream wrote something very short and very good to make that happen. I'd have liked to file it." He shut the folder. "A month's pay to read it. Two to know who sent the question to the man who wrote it."

Nobody asked him what he meant by that. He did not seem to expect them to.

They went out of the records hall into a bright cold noon, the four of them, and none of them spoke until they were halfway down the covered walk. Then Lira stopped, and turned, and hugged Karis. Hard, briefly, with one arm, as you would hug a teammate coming off a floor. Karis stood perfectly still inside it with her notebook held out to one side to keep it from being crushed, and her face went through three expressions in quick succession and settled on none of them.

"You'll make me drop the book," she said.

"You've never dropped a book in your life," said Lira, and let her go, and walked on.

By the evening the house had started moving again, all at once, as a mill wheel moves when somebody lifts the sluice.

Cael saw it in the order he had watched it stop. Rooke's first-meet targets went up on the calendar board in the clean space that had waited there for a fortnight, a full sheet in his small hard hand with a line for each of the five, and the line against Cael's name still said nothing but a dash. Bracken's clerk took the delegation's travel file out of its drawer and wrote a date on the cover sheet, at last, and blotted it, and showed it to Bracken, who looked at it and nodded as though a date were a thing that might still be got wrong. The wagoner was sent for, and came up from the town in his leather apron, and was told which morning, and went down again whistling. In the wing a new stack of the buff travel forms appeared at the counter's end, already filled in, five of them, in the round copying hand, each waiting only for a competitor's signature at its foot.

And Ephram, who had said nothing about the season in Cael's hearing for a fortnight, stopped him on the covered walk with his kit over his shoulder.

"Wool town," he said. "I've been there. My cousin's house fought at it, years back. The floors are pine. They give more than you'd think, on the left side of the main hall, where the old wall is." He hitched the kit. "Your hip will want to know that before your first burst, not after."

"Thank you."

"It's not kindness. If you go lame at the first meet I lose my sessions." He walked on, and then said over his shoulder, without turning, "The second-year entry. Every Iron fighter in that hall will have it. Watch the heel."

"I know."

"I know you know," said Ephram. "I'm telling you anyway, so it's said."

He wrote it at the rail of the Crown yard's top tier that afternoon, with the observation notebook on his knee and the porter below him chalking the first meet's date onto the long board in letters a hand high.

The fifth line of a printed card. Nobody signed it. Nobody will ever have to say they decided it, and no hearing will ever ask them to. If you'd told me at Greyvane that the best way to win a thing was to have it turn up in a timetable, I'd have written you down as a cynic.

It's also the line that frightens me, a little, and I want that in ink before I talk myself out of it. Somebody decided this. A question went up, and an answer came back, and somewhere between them a person chose to let it go through without a word to us or to the man who asked. The card is the shape the deciding left behind. I can hold the shape. I can't see the hand.

First paper in my life to call me Cael. A printer with two inches of column did that. I find I'm absurdly grateful to him, and I'll never know his name either.

He let it dry. Then, under it, in a smaller hand:

Thirteen days, Karis says, between the response going down and the card coming up. Long enough for an answer. Too long for an easy one.

He did not know quite why he wrote that, except that it was true to the feel of the thing, and he had learned to write down what a thing felt like before he knew what it meant. He blotted it and went down to the second training floor, where Ephram was waiting with a lath and a fresh grievance about his shoulders.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The slip Rooke laid on the bench in the map room was yellow with age, folded in four, and soft at the folds from being carried. Before he said a word about maps or brackets or roads, he unfolded it and held it up so that they could see it was real.

"My rating card," he said. "My last bout at the finals, my cycle. I lost it."

It was the first evening of the fifth week. The map room lay off the end of the second training floor, a long low chamber with no window and a north wall faced in cork, and every coach who had held the floor before Rooke had pinned something to that cork and left the holes. Rooke had cleared it that afternoon and pinned up four sheets of his own. There was the continent, with its coast and its rivers and its two hundred-odd chartered houses inked as dots. There was the region with its four meets ringed, and a bracket sheet with its tiers in columns, and at the end a close-ruled table of figures. The five of them sat in front of the sheets on a bench and two stools with the lamps behind them, and Rooke stood in front of the cork and showed them a piece of paper older than any of them.

"Read it," he said, and gave it to Karis, because Karis would read it aloud properly.

It was a printed form, filled in by hand. At the top, a floor number and a bracket: Iron. Two names, Rooke's and a stranger's. Below them a grid of fifteen boxes for each fighter, five rows by three columns, with a judge's initials at the head of each row and three words at the head of the columns.

"Execution," Karis read. "Control. Effect."

"Every bout at every meet is rated on those three," said Rooke. "Five judges. Each one gives each fighter three marks, one for each word. Look at my execution column."

Karis read it down. "Seven. Eight. Nine. Eight. Eight."

"Strike the highest and the lowest."

"The nine and the seven." She did it in her head. "Eight, eight, eight. Eight."

"Control."

"Eight, nine, nine, ten, nine. Strike the ten and the eight. Nine."

"Effect."

"Nine, eight, nine, nine, eight. Strike a nine and an eight. Eight point six six." She looked up. "Twenty-five point seven. Near enough."

"Twenty-six, they wrote. They round at the foot." Rooke took the card back. "Now his."

He handed it to Brom this time, and Brom read the other fighter's grid slowly, with his finger, and struck the high and the low, and did the sums with his lips moving, and came out at twenty-four.

"He won," said Brom.

"He won. Two touches to one, in the fourth exchange, on a feint I should have seen." Rooke folded the card along its old folds. "And the panel rated me two points higher than the man who beat me, because what I did on that floor was cleaner and better commanded and did more to him than what he did to me, until the one moment that mattered. The Standard rated what I did. It didn't rate what happened to me." He put the card away inside his coat. "That's the first thing to understand. It rates the performance. It doesn't rate the result."

He turned to the table at the end of the cork.

"Ten is par," he said. "A judge can mark past ten, all the way to fifteen, for work better than the mark; nobody in this room will see a fifteen given. But ten is par. Ten on each of the three, thirty in all, is what a practitioner at Silver tier and fifth rank does on an ordinary good day. Somebody measured that, a very long time ago, with a great many fighters and a great deal of care. It was witnessed and sealed. They lock it at the start of each cycle and nobody touches it until the cycle closes. Every judge on every panel is trained to that one picture and tested against it on old bouts, and struck off if they drift. They call it the Silver Standard."

He let them look at the table. It was a list of bands, read down from the top.

Thirty-five and above: Gold. Twenty-eight to thirty-four: Silver, with par at thirty in the heart of it. Twenty-two to twenty-seven: strong Iron to Silver-touched. Eighteen to twenty-one: Iron. Twelve to seventeen: Copper.

"A rating can run to forty-five," said Rooke. "Thirty is par, and Silver sits round it, a little below and a little above; Gold is what's left over the top." He laid a finger along the third line. "Bronze lives up here, across the top of that band. The tournament doesn't bracket Bronze, so you'll never see the word on a card."

"A good Copper bout rates in the low teens," said Rooke. "A sound Iron rates about twenty. If you rate twenty-three, every coach in the stand writes your name down. In the standings, the rating gets weighted by your bracket and by whether you won, so a Copper win and an Iron win can go into the same house total and mean what they ought to. Out of an exhibition, there's no weighting and no total. There's only the figure." He did not look at Cael. Everyone else did, briefly, and then looked back at the table. "The rest is the road."

He did the road in ten minutes, with the taped button of an old fencing foil, and Cael wrote it down without needing to. Four meets in the region; standings added; when a house's total crossed the region's line the registry would post a circular, and that house was going to the finals. The finals this cycle at Norhold, a crossroads city where four roads crossed a river, far to the north and east beyond the hill country: fourteen delegations or fifteen, out of all those dots. Brackets by tier, seeded by formal rank. A team trial for squads of five on a scenario floor. Exhibitions, voluntary, rated and worth nothing.

"By paper," said Lira, when he came to the seeding.

"By paper," said Rooke, without stopping.

When he had finished with the road he came back to the table and stood in front of it. His voice, when he went on, had dropped half a tone, the way it did perhaps twice a year.

"I've been in this trade a long time," he said. "I've seen floors bought. I've seen brackets drawn by men who owed money to the houses they were drawing. I've seen a certificate say Copper about a girl who could take any Iron in her region apart in four exchanges." Lira did not move. "This thing I've never seen lean. Not once. Rich houses have tried, for as long as anybody's kept books. Chief Adjudicator Umber keeps the calibration, and has done since before most of you were Kindled, and I've never heard a word against him that wasn't sour grapes from a house that lost." He tapped the table with one knuckle. "There are perhaps three honest instruments on this continent, and you're looking at one."

The lamps hissed.

"Who chose the three words?" said Karis.

Rooke turned his head.

"Execution, control, effect." She had her pencil against her lip. "Somebody chose those. Not four words. Not two. Not courage, or patience, or how long a fighter can stay on his feet, or how much he left in the bag." She was not arguing; she was reading, aloud, the way she read a charter. "I believe you about the mark. I believe nobody's caught it leaning. Once it's fixed, it's honest about everybody it measures. But somebody stood at the beginning of it and decided what was worth measuring, and everything after that is downhill from the deciding." She wrote one short line. "Nobody's ever described a fairer one to me. So was the sorting."

Rooke looked at her, and Cael watched him decide not to be offended.

"Both can be true," he said.

Rooke did not often spend philosophy, and he spent no more of it that night. He unpinned the road and rolled it, and turned to the matter of which of them would ride with the wagoner on the first day and who would walk.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Rooke's yellow card lay on the end of the bench when the others had gone.

Cael did not pick it up at once. He did not think Rooke left things on benches by accident, and he did not think Rooke would ever admit to having left this one on purpose, and both of those seemed to him to be the same kind of respect.

He unfolded it under the last lamp and read it the way Karis had, with the strikes, and got twenty-six for the loser and twenty-four for the winner, and sat looking at the two figures side by side.

Then he did a thing he would not have told anybody about. He turned the card over to its blank back, and with Hesk's pen he ruled a small grid of his own, five rows by three columns, and tried to fill it in for himself.

He could not. Not because he did not know what he could do; he knew to the burst. Because he did not know which of the things he could do he would let five strangers see. Execution, for a boy who ran the public suite at its documented rates and not one burst past them: clean, probably. Control: that depended on the man in front of him, and on whether the read, which looked from the stand like peculiar timing, would look to a trained panel like command. Effect: what the performance did. He could make a performance do almost anything a single exchange needed, if he spent what he owned. He would not spend it. So the figure in each box was not his; it was a choice. He sat with the pen over the grid and found he could write any number he liked in it, within a band, and that the band was his to choose, and that the instrument would never know.

He folded the card again along Rooke's old folds and put it back on the bench exactly where it had lain.

Then, because the habit was older than the doubt, he sat on the bench and priced the others. Lira, from what he had watched on the oak all recess: execution near nine, the cleanest bursts on the hill; control eight, nine against anyone slower than her; effect nine, because she made people spend. Twenty-six, perhaps. A Silver-touched figure for a girl whose certificate had said Copper not long ago. Brom: execution seven, because he would never look quick; control nine, because nobody moved Brom anywhere he did not agree to go; effect eight. Twenty-four. Ephram he had been rating in his head for a fortnight, and came out at twenty-four too. He did not price Karis. He did not know yet what an Ember fighter's effect looked like to a panel trained to Silver Five, and he found, to his surprise, that he wanted to be surprised by it.

At the window, with the fountain going below, he put it in the Log.

Rooke's card: a man who lost and was rated above the man who beat him. That's the whole of the Standard, and it's beautiful, and I sat in a cold room and admired it like a boy looking at a clock with its back off.

Here it is, plain, because I've been careful for a year not to write it: I want that figure. Not the standings; the standings aren't mine to want. The number. Three marks against par from five strangers who were trained to look at everybody the same way, and who will look at me the same way. Nobody has ever pointed a thing at me that was built for everyone. I want to stand in front of it and be measured like anyone. I want it more than I've let myself say anywhere until tonight.

He read that over, and let it stand. Then, because the honest ledger ran two columns, he wrote the other side under it.

And I'll only ever let it see what I choose to show it. I ruled a grid on the back of Rooke's card tonight and found I could fill it in with any figure in a band, and that the band was mine to pick. The fairest instrument on the continent, and I've already decided how to manage it.

He sat with his hand flat on the book in the dark, and did not like either line, and did not strike either of them out.

Chapter 6 — Par

[Quiet, purposeful narration; carry the earlier cost into the new campaign without recapping it]

Gault brought the case.

He came up the stair to the second training floor at the eighth bell of the Second-day carrying it in his right hand, a little away from his body, the way a man carries a thing he is proud of and does not want to seem proud of. It was a plain box of dark oak with brass corners and two brass catches, about the size of a ledger box, and on its lid, riveted through at either end, was a leather handle that had been stitched by somebody who cared about stitching.

Brom, who was sitting on the bench by the wall wrapping his hands, stopped wrapping them.

"That's the handle," he said.

"That is the handle," said Gault. He set the case down on the end of the judges' table and stood back to let Brom look at it. "Saddler's stitch. Double row. The man who made the frames sent it upriver with a note saying he'd been told I'd been issued a case and he would not have it said that any case of his trade went out with a cheap grip." He lifted the handle an inch, and let it fall back, and it settled without a sound. "I have no idea what to say to him. I've written him three drafts of a letter."

Brom got up, came across the floor, and lifted the case by the handle, once, about a foot off the table, and set it down again.

"Yes," he said, with deep seriousness. "I'd be pleased about that."

"Thank you," said Gault, just as seriously, and the two of them nodded to each other, and the matter appeared to be closed to the satisfaction of everybody concerned.

Rooke had changed the floor. The long room had a ring on it tonight, chalked in a circle about forty feet across, with a rope run round it at waist height on iron stands borrowed from the Crown yard. At the north side of the ring, outside the rope, stood a trestle with five chairs behind it and a lamp at each end, and in front of each chair lay a card printed with a grid of three columns and a pencil. The two third-year reserves were already there, the Shield reserve and the Stone, looking as though they had been told they were sitting an examination and had not been told the subject. Karis sat at the trestle's west end with the grey notebook beside her card. Rooke stood behind the middle chair with a book open in his hands.

It was an old book, thick, bound in a brown cloth that had faded nearly to grey, its spine broken in two places so that it fell open of its own accord.

"The examiner's manual," said Rooke. "My copy. My cycle. The adjudication office issues one to every panel, and every coach who ever fought under the Standard has stolen one." He laid it open on the trestle in front of the middle chair. "Tonight this floor is a meet floor and these five chairs are a panel. Two bouts. Each to two touches inside four exchanges, the way the meets run them. Each fighter rated by all five of us on the three words. Strike high, strike low, average the middle three, add the three columns, and I read the figure out loud where everybody can hear it."

"And the point?" said Lira, from the rope.

"The point," said Rooke, "is that in six days you'll stand in a ring with five strangers at a table, and they'll write three numbers about you that you'll never see them write, and you'll walk out of that ring not knowing why the figure was what it was. I'd rather you knew." He sat. "Enrollee. Ephram. You're first."

He gave them the rules in four sentences, because the meets would give them in forty. An exchange began on Rooke's word and ended on a clean touch, or a fighter out of the rope, or the sand running out in the glass at his elbow, whichever came first. A touch was clean if it landed with intent on the body, not the guard and not the limb that carried the guard, and the panel would say so if it was not. After each exchange both fighters went back to their chalk. "Two touches wins it," said Rooke. "If nobody has two after four exchanges, the panel's figures decide, and you'll find out tonight how little you'll enjoy that."

Gault took the chair at the trestle's east end. Before he sat he opened the case's catches, lifted out a pair of steel-rimmed spectacles he did not normally wear, put them on, and closed the case again.

"I'll mark what the manual says," he said to the table at large, "and not what I happen to know. I mention it so that it's in the room." He picked up his pencil. "I've been an evaluator for long enough to know how hard that will be."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

They came off their chalk marks at the far sides of the ring, and the first exchange began, and Cael found within a breath that he was fighting two things at once.

The first was Ephram, who knew what Cael had learned in ten days, and had spent those ten days learning what Cael read. He came straight off the mark with the second-year entry, front foot loaded, honest weight, the lath low; and Cael let the first share go by, and watched the heel, and the heel was flat, and flat, and then up, and he was already gone outside it. The lath passed a hand's breadth from his hip. Ephram did not seem surprised. He turned on the miss and came again, and this time the shoulders dropped with the front foot, everything at once, the plain entry, and Cael had to burst to get out from under it.

One burst. He counted it, as he would count every one tonight, aloud in his head. One. The leading hip took it, and the landing beat held him, a short locked pause on the far side of the ring, and he used the pause to look.

That was the second thing he was fighting: himself, and what he would let a panel see.

He had six free on the sprung oak. This floor was not the oak, it was the second floor's boards, a little stiffer, a little less forgiving, and he knew from a month of mornings that six here was really five. The record said he had a burst that carried twenty feet and a read that looked like peculiar timing. The record had nothing in it about a burst shut off halfway through its paying, or about a contact that took a blow and did not give it back, or about a plate. So tonight, in front of a panel of five, he would fight with what the record held, at the rates the record held it, and not one thing more. It was the doctrine, and he had chosen it, and he had never before had to keep to it in front of people holding pencils.

Ephram came across the ring.

Cael read him: weight forward, left, the shoulders not dropped, so the front foot only, so wait. He waited, and the heel came up, and he went right and outside, and as he went he put his palm on Ephram's ribs, a touch, clean, on the line the second weight had just left open, and stepped off.

"Touch," said Rooke, from the trestle. "Enrollee."

They went back to their marks.

The second exchange was long, and it was Ephram's, because he had learned from the first. He stopped throwing the second-year entry at all and began to walk, as he had walked on the morning of the first supervised session, at every angle and every pace, the lath low, never committing. The read told Cael everything about where Ephram's weight was going and nothing about when he would choose to send it. Twice Cael read a step as an entry and moved, and twice it was only a step, and he had moved for nothing, and had spent a little hip on each. Two. Three. On the third burst he landed close to the rope. Ephram, who had been walking him there for half a minute without either of them saying so, came in with all of it at once and laid the lath along his forearm as the landing beat held him still.

"Touch. Ephram."

Cael went back to his mark with his forearm stinging and his face doing nothing.

He knew what had happened, and he knew what he could have done about it. There was a thing in him that could take a blow along the forearm and swallow it whole; he had done it once at Ardenmere in front of six hundred people and a ledger. It was not on this house's record. So it had not happened, and the lath had landed, and that was the price of the doctrine, paid in one touch on a practice floor, and he set it down in his head in the column where such things went.

The third exchange he spent learning Ephram's walk. He did not move for any step that did not drop the shoulders, and he let three of Ephram's feints go by so close that he felt the air of the lath. Four was a burst that took him clear of the rope and into the open middle of the ring, where Ephram could not herd him. Then Ephram, who had worked out that Cael was now waiting for shoulders, threw a second-year entry with his shoulders held perfectly still. It was the thing he had been practising for ten days in front of the long window's glass. Cael read the front foot, and waited for a shoulder drop that never came, and nearly ate the second weight entirely. He got out of it by a hand. He did not get a touch back. The exchange ran out on Rooke's glass with nobody scored.

"Even," said Rooke.

In the fourth Cael stopped trying to read Ephram's choices at all. He read only his weight, the old way, the first way, early, and answered the first share of everything. Ephram, who had spent the bout teaching him to wait, could not believe he had stopped waiting, and threw the second-year entry three times running into a boy who was simply no longer where the second weight was meant to find him. On the third of them Cael went inside instead of out, under the lath, and laid his palm on Ephram's chest.

"Touch. Enrollee. Two to one. Bout to the enrollee."

They stood a moment in the middle of the ring, breathing.

"You stopped waiting," said Ephram.

"You taught me to wait. Then you taught me you'd teach everyone to watch me wait." Cael rubbed his forearm. "So I stopped."

Ephram's face showed, briefly, a craftsman's offence. Then he nodded.

"That's a good verdict," he said. "I'll take it."

Four bursts, Cael counted, walking to the rope. Four, on a floor where five was his limit, and nothing else: no contact taken. Nothing spent that was not already written down somewhere in a hand the registry could read.

He ducked under the rope, and sat on the bench, and watched the panel mark him.

Rooke read the cards out loud, as he had promised, and Karis did the striking, because she was quicker than any of them.

"Ephram. Execution: eight, eight, nine, eight, nine."

"Strike a nine and an eight," said Karis. "Eight, eight, nine. Eight point three three."

"Control: seven, eight, seven, eight, seven."

"Seven, seven, eight. Seven point three three."

"Effect: eight, eight, seven, eight, nine."

"Eight, eight, eight. Eight." Karis wrote it. "Twenty-three point six six. Twenty-four, rounded."

"Enrollee," said Rooke. "Execution: seven, eight, eight, eight, nine."

"Eight."

"Control: eight, eight, nine, nine, ten."

"Eight, nine, nine. Eight point six six."

"Effect." Rooke paused, very slightly, which in Rooke was the same as a man clearing his throat. "Six, seven, six, seven, six."

Karis's pencil stopped. Then it moved.

"Six, six, seven. Six point three three." She added. "Twenty-three. Exactly."

Ephram, sitting on the bench across the ring with a towel round his neck, looked from the trestle to Cael and back again, and his face went through a short and very private struggle.

"I lost," he said. "And I rated higher."

"By two-thirds of a point," said Rooke.

"I'll take the rating." Ephram put the towel over his head. "He can keep the bout. Fair trade." Then, from under the towel: "I'd still rather have the bout."

Lira laughed out loud at the rope, and the Stone reserve, who had not yet dared to laugh at anything in Rooke's presence, laughed with her and then looked as though he wished he had not.

Cael sat on the bench and did the sums again in his head, though Karis had done them right, because he wanted to see them work in his own hands.

Execution, eight, and that was fair. His feet had been clean and his bursts had been clean and his touches had been open palms on the right lines.

Control, eight and two-thirds. The panel had seen him own the middle of the ring and keep Ephram's lath out of it, and had marked it high, and he knew why: the read looked like command from outside the rope. It looked like decision. And at the same time, he knew, it had been a kind of trick. He had not decided where the bout would go. He had only known, half a beat early, where Ephram's weight was going, and been there first.

And effect, six and a third.

He looked at the three sixes and the two sevens on Rooke's cards, and understood them, and found that the understanding sat in his stomach like a cold stone.

They were right. Every judge at that table had marked exactly what had happened. He had won a bout without ever once making Ephram do anything Ephram did not already mean to do. Both his touches had been answers. He had not pressed, or driven, or taken ground that was not given; he had read, and arrived, and laid a palm on the space Ephram's own entry opened. The bout had been decided by what Ephram did, and by where Cael was standing when he did it. A panel trained to rate what a performance did had looked at that, honestly, five times over, and written six.

And he had chosen it. Every mark in that column was the price of a thing he had decided not to show, at a rate he had decided to keep.

"That's a strong Iron figure," said Rooke from the trestle. He was looking at the cards, not at Cael. "Twenty-three. Every coach in a stand would write your name down for it." He turned the cards face down. "You'll see it again."

At the trestle's west end Karis was turning the pages of Rooke's old manual, slowly, with one finger on the margin. She stopped somewhere about a third of the way in. She read a page there, and then she tore a narrow strip from the bottom of her own scoring card, and laid it in the manual at that page, and closed the book on it.

Cael saw her do it, and she saw him see her, and neither of them said a word.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Lira," said Rooke. "Brom."

They had not fought each other on a rated floor since the final, and both of them knew it, and neither of them said so. Lira went to her chalk with her wrists strapped and her face entirely calm. Brom went to his with the slow, settled walk he had when a thing was going to be heavy and he meant to carry it anyway. He had his right fist strapped; the knuckles had healed, but he strapped them now from habit, the way some men touch wood.

Cael stood at the rope with his arms on it and watched from outside, and for the first time in his life he watched a bout he was not in with a panel's eyes.

He did not know he was going to do it until it had begun. The first exchange opened, and Lira came off her mark in a burst that took her twenty feet down Brom's left side, and without deciding to, Cael thought: execution, nine. It was clean. It was so clean it was almost dull; there was no wasted hand, no wasted step, the landing beat she owned was a sliver of what his own was, and she was moving again before Brom had finished turning. Brom turned, and planted, and took her next burst's shoulder on his forearm at the end of its run and gave it back to her, and Cael thought: control, Brom, eight. Effect, eight. Not because Brom had won the moment but because he had made Lira's burst cost her something it had not been meant to cost.

He found he could see the figures forming. Not as numbers in his head, exactly. As a kind of weight on each thing that happened, the way the read put weight on a step before the step was finished. He had spent a month learning what a panel's ten looked like from a table in a map room. Now, outside the rope, he could see par walking about on the floor in front of him, and see where these two came close to it and where they did not.

Lira came close. She came closer than anybody on the hill. In the second exchange she spent three bursts in the time Brom spent one turn, and took him on the shoulder on the third, and walked back to her mark without looking at the trestle at all.

Brom came close in a different place, though he never once looked fast. But in the third exchange, which went long, he did a thing Cael had watched him rebuild across a whole season of Rooke's sheets: he took one of Lira's bursts on the struck side, hard, and did not finish absorbing it before he drove. The seam was gone. The drive came while she was still landing, and his forearm touched her ribs, and Rooke said "Touch, Brom," in the same voice he used for everything.

Lira stood on her mark after that, and then smiled, briefly, at Brom across the ring. It was not a pleasant smile. It was the smile of a fighter who has been reminded of a thing and is grateful.

She took the fourth exchange. It was not close.

Cael watched how she did it, and for the first time understood it from where a panel would sit. She did not chase Brom. She went to the corners of the ring, one after another, and made him turn to face her at each one. Each turn cost him a little of the ground under his feet, because a man as heavy as Brom does not turn in his own length, while each burst cost her almost nothing. By the third corner Brom was standing on the rope side of the middle with nowhere left to plant. Lira did not even need her fourth burst. She walked in on the third turn's last step, while his weight was still coming round, and laid her palm on his shoulder, very gently. It was the touch a groom gives a horse to tell it he is there.

Control, nine, Cael thought, before Rooke had picked up a single card. Effect, nine. She made him spend his ground. He didn't give it to her; she took it. It was the very thing his own column had lacked, set out in front of him in four bursts, by the person who had taught him what a burst was.

Rooke read the cards. Karis struck them.

"Lira. Twenty-six point three three. Twenty-six."

There was a small silence along the trestle. The Shield reserve looked at his own card again, to be sure he had really written what he had written.

"Brom. Twenty-three point six six. Twenty-four."

Brom, who had been unwinding the strapping from his right fist, stopped.

"That's the same as Ephram," he said.

"It's the same as Ephram," said Rooke.

"I'm Copper."

"You're Copper on your certificate," said Rooke. "You rated twenty-four tonight against an Iron Rank One with a panel of five, two of whom have never once said a kind word about anybody." The reserves did not look at each other. "The Standard doesn't read certificates. That's the whole of what I've been telling you."

Brom went on unwinding the strap, slowly, and wound it into a neat roll, and put the roll in his pocket. Then he said, to the floor, very quietly:

"That's a number a stranger reads."

Nobody answered him. Lira came across the ring and sat down on the bench beside him, close, with her shoulder against his, and stayed there; and Cael, at the rope, wrote nothing at all, because some things were better left as a space.
