He wrote the day in the old volume first, because the old volume was still the one he lived in.

It was nearly full, and he had known for weeks that it would run out somewhere on the road home, and he had been rationing it, a few lines a day, small. Tonight he gave it four. Rest day. The blue door, all six. Brom's cake, paid three days early. Seln at the table. He looked at the last three words for a while, and did not add anything to them, and shut the book.

Then he opened Hesk's.

He had not written in it yet. He had carried it back from the harbour under his arm, the whole length of the quays, and up the stair, and set it on the table under the window, and walked round it twice, and had a wash, and come back, and it was still there. It lay open in the middle by itself, as it had at the cookshop. He turned back to the first leaf. The paper took the lamp's light softly and gave nothing back.

Every new book of accounts begins by saying what is in the till. Hesk had taught him that before he could spell accounts.

He wrote slowly, in his best hand, with Hesk's steel pen.

Seventeen. The first page of Hesk's book, on the rest day in the middle of the sitting. Kept at the blue door by everybody who matters, and written here by me, as I was taught to write down the numbers nobody else was keeping. Somebody kept this one. That's the first thing this book knows.

What I carry, at seventeen. Six, and the one I can't account for.

Lira's burst. Six free on the sprung oak; four a day on this city's stone. Against Rhagen I ran eleven relocations in one exchange and only two of them were bursts. Feet carried the rest. The landing beat is no shorter than it was at the year's open.

The push I took from the Bronze at Ardenmere. Flat on two plates on the bluff and one in a felt bag at the mill town. Four blows a sitting, paid in the right shoulder. Not asked for since the mill town's plate.

Brom's read. Weight and direction, early. Against both Silvers it was the one thing I never ran short of. It can't see a weave, and it can't see a price. It sees what's heavy.

Reydan's give. Not on a scored floor since Ardenmere. Nobody official has seen it. I held it still at a handspan, twice, in a pocket of stone at the north gate with a Silver's hand coming down. It would have worked. It stays where it is.

Karis's spark, by her leave, in her hand. Four instants on a copper pot. Two contacts a bout on a public floor, which is our rule, not theirs. Both spent on Rhagen, both on purpose. Four days of a pink hand.

The quiet thing from the stair. A year, near enough. Never used, anywhere, by anyone's count. Rent from waking, spent or not. Drifts in the gaps, never in the work, fewer this month than last. Useful where: nowhere yet. Still the second year of that answer.

And at the foot of the list, the still place from session nine. I turned it over again tonight, as I do at every opening and every closing, to see whether I can call it back or say why it came. I can't do either.

Still open. Still real. Patience.

One stamp, renewed. One enrollment, lawful. Half a tournament behind me and half to come. And the entry I wrote at the window after the captain, which has no answer yet and isn't going to get one by being copied out again. This book can carry it from here.

He sat back and let the ink dry in the tooth of the paper.

It looked right. It looked like a page that would still be there to argue with in a year, and he found, reading it over, that he had already found one line he wanted to argue with, and that the narrow ruled margin was exactly the right width to do it in. He did not write in the margin, not tonight. He shut the book on its first page and put his hand on the cover, and then went down, because the draw posted at dusk and nobody read a draw alone.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

The outer court was full by the time they came down into it, and it was still filling.

The Concourse's canvas had come off in the late afternoon, and the city had stretched itself and begun to remember that it was a tournament town. Lamps were being lit along the colonnades. The criers were back in the betting rows under their awnings. On the platform at the court's north side the drum stood on its iron spindle, and the three clerks from the west tower stood beside it, and in front of them, on a board, the trial's printed frame waited with its four lines blank.

Only four houses would field a squad. That had been on the trial rules since the fourth morning, and the standings had settled which four: the houses highest on the count as it stood when the brackets reached their finals. Auremont was first, by a long way. Rhagen was second. Halcenvane, on Brom's title and two semifinals and a quarterfinal over Ternhall's best, had come in third, a long way behind Rhagen and a hand ahead of the river academy.

Four squads, then, and two semifinals. The beaten pair would meet for third place on a later day, and the winners would meet in the final.

The marshal turned the drum.

He did it as he had done it on the night of the brackets' draw, holding each slip up in the lamplight for one long breath before he read it, and the court drew its breath with him every time.

The first slip was Rhagen. The second was the river academy.

Then the third, and Cael heard Lira beside him stop breathing.

"Halcenvane," said the marshal. He reached into the drum for the last slip, which everybody in the court could have told him, and held it up anyway, for the custom. "Auremont."

The clerk wrote it on the board in white. HALCENVANE — AUREMONT.

For a moment the court was quiet in a way Cael had not heard it be quiet before. Then it was not quiet at all. It ran across the square from the board outward, faster than any crier could have carried it. People at the front read it aloud to the people behind them, and the people behind them turned round and said it to the next, and by the time it reached the colonnades on the far side it had been worn down to two words, and then, as he listened, to one, which was Auremont, said in a great many different tones of voice.

He watched the houses read it. Rhagen's people read their line and were very obviously relieved, and were far too well brought up to let anybody in plain colours see them be relieved, and went off toward their quarter talking quickly and quietly among themselves. The river academy's coaches read it twice. Then, at the foot of the far colonnade, a cup went up. It rose only a little way and stayed there. Cael followed it down to the hand that held it, and the hand to a russet sleeve: one of two Ternhall Irons, beaten out of the bracket days ago and staying on in the city to watch, who had gone looking through the crowd for plain colours and found them. She did not drink until she was sure they had seen.

Cael knew what that meant. Everybody at a tournament knew. It meant better you than us, and it meant go on anyway, and both meanings were sincere.

Along the west side of the court a crier's voice went up under an awning, and then another. The little framed sign still hung at the end of the long row of chalked boards, where it had hung all sitting, in neat white paint. NO BOOK ON THE DEMONSTRATION BOUTS. Cael read the boards above it. Auremont to win the semifinal, at a price so short it was hardly a price at all. Auremont to take the final. How many exchanges the semifinal would run. And two of the criers, who had read the little sign as often as anybody, had begun to cry it as a selling point.

"No price on the fifth man of the bluff! None! The house won't quote him! Come and see the thing we can't price!"

"They've made you a feature," said Ephram.

"They've made me a hole in their board," said Cael.

Nobody else said what everybody in the court was thinking. Auremont had not filed its squad yet. When it did, whatever else the list held, it would hold the Gold, and there was no rule anywhere in the trial's pages to keep her off the floor. A scenario floor had no tiers on it. It had ground, and the people each house sent out to stand on the ground.

Karis had gone back to the guesting-house on the way down from the harbour, for a quarter of an hour, alone. Nobody had asked her why. Now she took her notebook out of her coat, the grey one, and opened it to the page she had shown Cael at this same board on the fourth morning, and spread it open on the rail below the board, under the torch, so that all five of them could read it.

Squads shall be drawn from the academy's roster. Its number in the rules. A line drawn down to an older line from the front of the book. Participating academies shall field any practitioner appearing on their enrollment record. Sixth part. Subsection four. And under both, the one word.

Again.

She looked at the place on the rail where Withrow was standing, with Bracken a step behind her and the travel pouch under Bracken's arm. Then she looked at Cael. The torch over the board flared in the evening wind and settled.

"You're on the roster," she said. "The clause does the rest. Again."

Withrow had read the page over Karis's shoulder.

She took a slip of paper and a pencil from Bracken, and wrote on the slip against the board's frame, in her clear upright hand, five names and the number of a rule. Cael, Lira, Brom, Karis, Ephram. She did not add a sentence. She did not add the clause, or the year's arguments, or anything at all that a clerk might read as somebody expecting a quarrel.

"A filing with an argument stapled to it is a filing that thinks it will lose," she said. "This one doesn't think anything. It's a list."

She took it across the court herself to the west tower's night clerk, who sat at a table under the colonnade for exactly this purpose with a lamp and a book, and handed it to him, and watched him enter it, and came back.

"Filed," she said. "Go to bed. All of you. Rooke wants you at the second bell." She looked at Cael. "And happy birthday."

He wrote the second entry in Hesk's book that night, under the inventory, with the window open and the court still murmuring below.

Seventeen. Six fragments. Tomorrow I find out if the second technicality holds, and if it does — the found family fights together, on a sanctioned floor, for the first time in any of our lives. Whatever else this tournament is for, it was for that.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Rooke did not wait for the second bell.

He sent Ephram round the rooms an hour after the draw to fetch them all to the hired hall behind the east tower. When they got there he had lamps lit along the trestle and five sheets of paper laid face up across it, and the trial's printed rules pinned on the wall above them, and he did not look as if he had any intention of letting anybody go to bed.

"Withrow's filed," he said. "Somebody in the west tower will decide in the morning whether they like it. I'm not going to spend a night waiting to find out what a clerk thinks. We'll plan it as filed, and if they say no, I'll have wasted an evening, and I've wasted worse."

He put his hand on the rules.

"I'll say how it's scored once, so we're all saying the same thing tomorrow. Four exchanges, each by the timekeepers' glass. Three platforms on the floor. While one house stands on a platform alone, the platform marshals count it in quarter-minutes, and the quarter-minutes go in a column they call the objective ledger. The flags count clean touches, as they always do, in the other column. A fighter who's touched goes back to his own gate and puts his hand on the post before he comes back on. Whichever house has more quarter-minutes in an exchange takes the exchange. If the exchanges come out even, the whole objective ledger decides." He took his hand off the sheet. "That's all of it. It's a game about ground, and the touches are how you take the other side's people off the ground for a while."

He turned to the sheets.

"Five names. The ones I've got answers for first."

The first sheet was the lattice-breaker.

"Karis," said Rooke. "He's yours again. You know his sums. He takes things apart for a living, and he's patient about it, and he's very good." He tapped the sheet. "So give him things to take apart. On ramps we don't need. Let him walk into every one of them, and make every one cost him a minute he'll want back."

Karis nodded. Her palms were a week old now, pink and shiny at the heel, and she held them a little open on the table in front of her.

"Your hands," said Rooke.

"Can carry a frame," said Karis. "They can't carry raw contact. Not all afternoon." She looked down at them. "I'll plant. All three anchors, every time, the long way. The frame takes the heat down where it ought to go. I won't be quick." She looked up. "I'll be expensive."

"That'll do," said Rooke.

The second and third sheets were Auremont's two Silver seniors, a man and a woman, and Rooke laid them side by side.

"These two have fought trials for ten years between them. They've won most of them. They play the objective game exactly as it's written, in order, and they don't make mistakes, and they never, ever do anything that isn't in a book." He looked down the trestle. "Ephram."

"Yes."

"They're yours. You'll be calling against them all afternoon. They'll do the right thing every time, and they'll do it on time." Rooke folded his arms. "So you do one thing, once, when it counts, that's not in any book they've ever read. I don't know what it is. You'll know."

Ephram did not answer. He looked at the two sheets for a long time.

The fourth sheet was Zerin.

"Lira," said Rooke.

He said nothing else. Lira nodded without looking at the sheet. There was nothing on it that she did not already know by heart, and she had already lost to the woman whose name was at the top of it, honestly, in front of eight thousand people, and she was going to spend everything she had learned.

Rooke picked up the fifth sheet.

He did not read it. He turned it over and laid it down again, blank side up, and rested his palm on it.

"I've no plan for her," he said.

Nobody said anything.

"I've watched every minute of her that a man could watch in this city. I can tell you what she does. She finds whatever on a floor is least able to bear her, and goes there, and it doesn't bear her." He kept his hand where it was. "Stopping it isn't a thing any five of you can do, and I won't pretend to you it is."

He looked round at them.

"So here's the only thing I know. That ledger counts the whole floor for the whole of every exchange. Every platform, every minute, all five of us and all five of them. She's very good, and she's one person. She can't be everywhere on a floor at once." He tapped the back of the sheet, once. "We win the places she isn't. As long as we can. That's the plan."

He lifted his palm away. The sheet lay where it was, blank side up, and none of them reached to turn it.

The trial clerk brought the list up the west tower at the first bell of the morning, while the Chief Adjudicator was still standing at the window of the long room with his first cup.

Umber had been up since before light, as he usually was during a sitting. Through the gallery screen at the far end of the room he could see down onto the main floor, and he had stood there for most of an hour watching the crews take the exhibition ring down by lamplight. The posts had come out of the sockets one at a time, each eased up out of its hole with a long bar while two men held it, and been laid on the barrows. The planking had gone. The rope had gone. Then the plugs had gone back into the sockets, one by one, and an old woman on an upturned barrow had oiled each of them before it went in, and the crews had begun, at the far end of the oval, to bring in the timber for the trial terrain.

He found he had liked watching it. A floor was a floor. It held whatever stood on it, and the oil did not care who.

"The Halcenvane squad, Chief Adjudicator," said the clerk. He was a tall careful man with ink on his second finger, and he held the slip as if it might go off. "Filed at dusk with the chancellor's signature. Five names and the rule's number. Nothing else."

Umber put down his cup and took the slip.

He read the names, and knew all five. He had watched two of them on the main floor from behind this very screen, and he had read the figures of the other three every evening for two weeks, and the fifth name had been on his desk in one form or another since the fourth morning of the sitting, when the trial rules went up on the board and he had read the rule's single sentence and known exactly what somebody would do with it.

The trial office's two senior clerks had come up the stair behind the first, and his own deputy behind them, and they stood in a row at the end of the long table and waited. Somebody had put the rules on the table already, open at the page.

Umber read it aloud, once.

"Squads shall be drawn from the academy's roster."

He let it stand in the room for a moment, as he let every rule stand, so that everybody present had heard the whole of it and nothing but it.

"The rule says roster," he said. "A house's roster is whatever its enrollment book says it is. That book was certified at the start of this year by the house's own registrar. A regional office questioned it, was answered, and printed it." He laid the slip on the open page. "There is nothing to rule on. There's only a list."

"There will be talk," said the senior of the two clerks.

"There's talk now. There will be talk tomorrow whatever I sign this morning." Umber looked down at the slip. "Gentlemen, for two weeks this office has rated that boy under a provision three hundred years old that nobody alive had used before this sitting, on a frame we had to have repainted, by a panel we had to convene. We rated him correctly. I've seen every figure. But every figure was one we built a room for, after he'd arrived in it."

He put his finger on the rule.

"The trial is rated on what a squad does together, against the Standard, on tables this office has used every cycle for longer than any of us has been alive. It has a column for every fighter on the floor. It doesn't ask what any of them are. It asks what they did." He looked up. "For the first time in this sitting, I'd be rating him on a sheet that was already built to hold him, in a column that was already there. I would like that very much. I would like it a great deal more than whatever this office will have to invent if I find a reason to say no."

Nobody spoke.

"Approve it before somebody makes me invent something," said Umber.

The deputy wrote. The senior clerk sealed the approval and took it away down the stair, and the junior clerk followed him, and the deputy went after them both.

Umber picked up his cup again. The tea had gone cold. He drank it anyway, standing at the gallery screen, looking down at the main floor, where the crews were laying out the first long line of the trial's barrier across the stone, from one corner of the floor toward the other, in the early light.

Bracken collected the notice himself from the trial office at the second bell, and brought it up the guesting-house stair to the long table, where they were all eating breakfast, and laid it down beside the bread.

It was one sheet, sealed, and it said that the Halcenvane squad was approved as filed.

"Within the hour of opening," said Bracken. "I'm told the Chief Adjudicator read the rule aloud once and approved it without a hearing." He sat down, which he rarely did at their table, and took a piece of bread, which he more rarely did. "I'm also told he was relieved. The trial office wants it known that it was not relieved, being an office, but that he was." He buttered the bread with great precision. "I don't mind telling you I was relieved myself. I've been sleeping badly on that clause for a year. Last night I slept like a quarry stone." He considered. "That's twice since the bluff. I may be getting used to it."

By the third bell the notice was on the boards in the outer court. HALCENVANE — SQUAD AS FILED.

The broadsides had it by the fourth. The criers had a new thing to shout. And the Concourse's ticket office, which had sold the semifinal's rails in the first hour after the draw, sold its standing room by the middle of the morning and shut its window and put up a board that said NONE, which nobody in the city could remember seeing at a semifinal before.

They walked the floor at the end of the morning, in the quarter of an hour the charter gave each squad, and they walked it apart, each to the part of it that belonged to them.

The crews had worked all night, and the main floor was no longer an oval of grey stone with a round of oak in the middle. It was country. It ran ninety feet from end to end, west to east, fenced at its edges with low rails, with Halcenvane's gate at the west end and Auremont's at the east. From the north-west corner of the floor clear across to the south-east ran one long barrier of heavy timber, head-high and straight as a ruled line, so that the floor was cut on the slant into two long triangles. Halcenvane's gate opened into the southern one, and Auremont's into the northern.

There were three platforms, each a low square of planking knee-high with a ramp at either end. Two stood in the northern triangle, in Auremont's country, one toward each end of it. The third stood alone in the southern triangle, in Halcenvane's, tucked far down toward the south-east corner. At both ends of the barrier the crews had stacked timber head-high in thick clusters to spoil the view across the corners, and just south of the barrier's middle, untouched, lay the old oak round, a dark disc in the stone.

Lira went first, because she could not stand still. She ran the northern triangle from end to end and then the southern, at three-quarter pace, with the heat-wrap gone from her left arm for the first time in a week and the arm carried a little close. When she came back to the west gate she was hardly breathing.

"North's quick," she said. "Open floor, new boards over the stone, nothing in the way. South's the old patched stuff, and the platform down there is behind a stack with a long ramp each side. It'll take two of us to keep it, and it's only worth what one of the north ones is worth." She wiped her hands on her shirt. "Fast north, slow south. That southern one costs double what it scores."

Rooke had his sheet on his knee at the rail. He looked at Lira over the top of it, and then, without a word, drew one short line under something he had written there already.

Karis did not run anything. She went and stood on the ramp of the north-west platform with her arms folded and her pink palms tucked into her elbows, and then on the ramp of the north-east one, and then she walked back slowly, looking over her shoulder the whole way.

"From up there you can't see the middle of the barrier," she said to Ephram. "The stacks are in the way, both ends. Any call you make from a northern ramp, you make without seeing where it lands." She considered it. "Auremont's caller has the same trouble from the same ramps. Whoever plans for it before the other one does gets a minute free. Count out loud when you're behind a stack. Then we'll know where you are even if we can't see you."

Brom had gone to the barrier. He did not look at it much. He leaned on it, every few strides, the whole length of it, the way a man leans on a fence to find the post that gives. Twice he stopped and turned sideways and put his shoulder into a place where the barrier was not, and came back out. When he had done the whole length he walked back to the gate.

"Two gaps," he said. "At two of the joins. The first's about a third of the way along from our end. The second's forty feet past it." He held up one big bandaged hand. "One man through either at a run. Not two together. Not if they want to keep their elbows."

He did not say which of the gaps he meant to stand in. Nobody needed him to.

Cael walked it last, on his own.

He walked the triangles and the ramps and the slow southern stone, and he found everything the others had found and agreed with all of it. But the thing he kept coming back to, without any reason he could give, was the barrier.

Everybody who walked this floor, he thought, would walk it as a wall. It was the thing you went through the gaps of, or round the ends of, the thing that split the country in two. He stood at its north-west end and sighted down its face. It ran from that corner to the far one without a break, smooth and straight, ninety-odd feet of it. Nothing else on the floor was that long. Nothing else ran from one end of the fight to the other.

The read had nothing to say about it. The read saw weight, and the barrier's weight was not going anywhere.

He wrote it down all the same, in the column of the notebook where he kept things he could not use yet. The diagonal. Corner to corner, unbroken. Longest line on the floor. Everybody's reading it as a wall. He looked at it, and added one more line under it. The feature nobody has priced.

Then he put the notebook away. Gault was waving at him from the gate with the tape, and he went.

The fifth name went up on the board at the noon bell, after the other four, in the same white chalk as the rest.

Nobody had made much of the first four. The clerk had chalked them in the order of the filing: the lattice-breaker, the heavy patient Force fighter who had taken Karis apart six days before; Zerin; and two names Cael knew only from Rooke's sheets, a man and a woman, Silvers from the deep end of Auremont's program, with ten years of team trials between them and few losses in any of them.

The bowl did not shout her name. It said it, all of it at once, eight thousand people in one long low breath, and then it was quiet for a moment, and then it began to roar.

Cael stood at the west gate with the others and listened to the roar and read it, because reading things was what he did when he was frightened. Under it he could hear two hopes at once, the holders' and the bluff's, shouted by the same people in the same breath. The holders against the house with the blank. The Gold against the boy nobody could rate. He did not write any of it down. There would be no time for writing on that floor.

Rooke's team talk was four sentences long.

He stood at the gate with his coaching sheet folded small in one fist, and looked at the five of them, and at the Shield reserve standing behind them in his kit as the squad's alternate, white to the lips.

"You've been a squad on every floor I've put you on," said Rooke. "Today somebody counts it." He put the sheet in his pocket. "That's all. Go on."

The referee brought the ten of them to the middle of the floor for the presentation, five on each side of the old oak round, with the long barrier running away behind them toward both corners.

Auremont stood in deep blue and silver, the house every broadside in the city called the favourites, with more titles behind it, over more cycles, than anybody could easily count. Halcenvane stood in plain colours. Lira, with her left arm carried close. Brom, with his forearms rewound in fresh linen for the afternoon. Karis, with her pink palms turned a little outward. Ephram, at the end of the line, already counting something under his breath. Four exchanges by the glass. A touched fighter to his own gate and the post. Cael did not listen. He was watching Daeva.

She stood at the end of Auremont's line, opposite him, a pace away. She was tall, as he had seen at a hundred yards, and close to she was younger than she had looked at a hundred yards, and quite still. She did not look at him. She did not look at any of them.

She was looking at the floor.

He watched her eyes go over it while the referee talked. They went to the platforms, one, two, three, briefly. To the timber stacks at the barrier's ends. To the gaps Brom had found, both of them, as if she had found them too. They stayed there longer than they had stayed on anything.

The referee finished. The ten of them bowed to the dais, and to one another, and walked back to their gates.

The first exchange went to the house that had never been counted.

It took Cael the first minute to see that it would, and the rest of the exchange to believe it. It showed from the opening call, before anybody in the tiers had a word for it. Fighter for fighter, the five in blue were the better five, and nobody in the building thought otherwise, least of all the five in plain colours. What Halcenvane had that afternoon, for that exchange and the one after it, was a squad.

At the first call Auremont went for every platform on the floor. It was the right opening, the one every house in the trial had always run, and they ran it well. The lattice-breaker and one of the Silvers came out of the east gate, round the barrier's south-east end past the timber stack, and down into Halcenvane's country toward the south platform. The other three went for the two northern platforms in their own triangle.

Ephram said one word.

"North."

Halcenvane went north. All five of them crossed into Auremont's country, some through the first gap in the barrier and some round its western end, and not one of them so much as looked at the south platform. The lattice-breaker and the Silver came down the long ramp onto it, and found nobody there to fight them for it, and stood on it.

It counted. It counted the same as either of the northern ones. But it had taken two of Auremont's five to get there, and it would take two of them to stay, and it was the farthest thing on the floor from everywhere that mattered.

Cael saw the Silver on the south platform understand it. The man stood at the top of the ramp for one full second doing visible sums, and then stayed, because a platform with nobody on it is a platform you hold, and the book said so.

That was Lira's sentence from the morning, spent inside the first minute.

The rest of it was the squad.

Cael ran the middle. He had no platform of his own. He stood a little north of the barrier between the two northern ramps, where he could see across the open ground, and he read the traffic. He read weight and direction and where every fighter on the floor was going a fraction before they went, the ordinary read, the thing his file called peculiar timing, and he gave it out to the others in single words. The five of them had been growing those words for a year at tables and on floors, until they were almost a language of their own. Left. Back. Two coming. Gap. Nobody else in the building could have understood half of it.

Brom went to the second gap and stood in it.

He did nothing else for the whole exchange, and nothing else was needed. Auremont's pair on the south platform were in the wrong country. Sooner or later the north would want them back, and short of the barrier's far ends there were exactly two holes in it, and one of them now had Brom in it like a cork in a bottle. The Silver tried it first. He came at the gap fast from the south side, saw what was standing in it, and stopped and went back, because there is no going through a gap that is already full. A little later he tried it again, and Brom's heavy hand found his shoulder in the gap's mouth, and the flag went up, and the Silver had to walk all the way to Auremont's gate to touch the post. After that nobody in blue used the second gap at all. They went round by the south-east stack instead, nearly the whole length of the floor, and the platform marshals counted every minute they spent on the way.

Karis took the north-east ramp.

She went up it slowly and planted her three anchors at its head, one, two, three, in the fixed order Ternhall had taught her and she had walked away from and come back to: the leading foot, a stride forward on the line, the flank. Then she stood in her frame with her pink palms open. She was not quick, and she did not try to be. But anybody who wanted the north-east platform had to come up that ramp, and anybody who came up that ramp had to come within reach of her hands. Any contact she made went down through her planted feet into the planking, where the frame sent it, and not back into her palms.

One of the Silvers came up the ramp at her early in the exchange. She lit at contact on his forearm. He went down the ramp again with the flag going up, back to his gate, and the next one who looked at that ramp looked at it a long time.

When they did come, they came round the platform's blind side, away from the ramp, and Lira was already there.

She had been there for half a beat. Cael had read the man's weight shifting to go round and said one word, and Lira had said one back, without stopping, the word she and Cael had worn smooth between them on a waystation's clay a month before.

"Early."

She spent one burst on it, from the boards on the north triangle's open ground, and arrived at the corner of the platform before the Silver did, and touched him on the shoulder as he came round it.

Up in the tiers the sound had changed. People who had paid to watch two famous fighters had begun, without quite knowing it, to watch five ordinary-looking ones move as if they shared one pair of eyes.

Auremont changed in the interval.

It took them two minutes, and they did it calmly, and that frightened Cael more than anything he had seen in the first exchange. A house that could look at what had just happened to it and rebuild the whole of its game between two bells was a house that did not need to be frightened of anybody.

The lattice-breaker went straight for Karis.

He did it as he had done it in the bracket, methodically, out in the open, so that everybody could see the method. He walked up her ramp. He let her light at him, and the flag went up, and he went back to his gate and touched the post and came back and walked up the ramp again. He was not trying to win the ramp. He was trying to break the frame.

He knew what a frame was. He had made his name taking them apart. Every time he walked into her, she had to light, and every time she lit, the frame had to take the heat, and the frame had been planted once and was being paid for again and again. On the third walk Cael saw her anchor foot shift. On the fourth he saw her face.

The two Silvers would not go near Brom's gap. It was the correct answer, and they had ten years of trials behind it, and it held. The price of it was distance. To stay out of the gap they had to go round the barrier's ends, and the ends were a long way off, and every time they went round, the northern triangle was a pair short.

Daeva did her part.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Ilsev had been writing steadily since the first call.

She sat in the first seat of the Compact's row with the observation form for the team trial laid on her lap-desk, and she wrote as she always wrote, in the even hand her office had trained into her over a great many years, a line for every event the form had a place for. The form had ten columns, one for each fighter on the floor, five a side. At the head of each column the office's clerk had copied the fighter's name and house and the registry's classification, so that an observer could weigh what she saw against what the registry said she ought to be seeing.

Nine of the columns had a tier at the head of them. The tenth had the registry's word for him, in its square brackets, as it was printed on every paper about him in the Compact's files.

She had written the registry's word herself on her own forms more times than she could count. She had written beside it, every time, on every form she had ever filed concerning him, the same short note about the watch level on his sheet. Authorizing office: not traced. She had written it on a referral, once, and then on a second referral, and the second was still pending somewhere above her desk.

She had written the first exchange into the ten columns as it happened. Touches, positions, platform holds, the quarter-minutes as the marshals called them. It had been perfectly possible. It was what the form was for.

It was in the second exchange that the form began to go wrong.

Not wrong. Ilsev did not use that word lightly, and the form was not wrong. Everything she wrote in it was true. But she found, partway through the second exchange, that she was writing the same event into four columns and then into a fifth. The big Copper in the gap had not stopped the Silvers. He had cost them a stride, and the Ember girl's frame had cost them a ramp, and the Wind girl had been on the far side of the ramp half a beat early, and the girl had been sent there by a single word from the boy in the middle. The caller had made a trade on the north-east platform that she would have marked, if she had been examining a cadet, as an error.

There was no column on the form for that. The thing that was happening on the floor did not belong to any one of the five fighters in plain colours. It belonged to all of them at once, and her form had no place to put a thing that belonged to five people.

At the bell for the end of the second exchange, her pen stopped.

She looked down at it. It had stopped in the middle of a line, in the fifth column, under the registry's word.

She did not start it again at once. She sat with it lifted a little off the page and looked at the floor, where the five in plain colours were walking back to their gate, and she was aware, very precisely, as she was aware of everything in her own conduct, that she had never in her working life stopped writing at an interval because she did not know what to write.

Along the row, past Havel and the rotating seats, the twelfth chair stood empty again behind its rail-cloth. The Archmarshal had been in it two days before, for one bout. He had written twice and gone. She had not spoken to him. Nobody in the row had. She found herself wondering, for no reason she could have put in a report, whether he would have wanted to see this, and what he would have written in a book with no columns in it at all.

The referee called the squads to their gates.

Ilsev looked at the half-finished line under the bracketed word, and left it as it was, and turned to a fresh line for the third exchange.

The third exchange began at the barrier's south-east end, and Cael felt it before anybody on the floor saw anything at all.

Daeva had come out of the east gate with the others, as she had in the first two, and gone round the end of the barrier past the timber stack into the corner. For one breath the read, which had only ever read bodies, gave Cael the feeling of weight somewhere there was no body at all: a heaviness laid along the whole face of the timber, from her corner toward the far one, as though the air beside the wall had been pressed flat and was waiting to snap back.

Then she was in it.

She did not run along the barrier. Cael would think about the word for a long time afterward, and run was not it. The air along the timber's face folded, all the way down its length, into a long narrow lane, and she went down the lane as a stone goes down a well. There was a crack at its head like a whip, and a smell like a struck flint, and a pale flicker of light that was gone before he could look at it. She covered the barrier's length faster than anything on the tables of any tier he had ever read.

And all at once the whole floor was something else.

It was not that Halcenvane's game had been beaten. It had been stepped over. The gaps Brom had priced, the ramps Karis had made dear, the corners Lira bought early and the calls Ephram counted from behind the stacks: every one of them was a thing that happened on the floor. They were roads and gates and tolls. The lane did not use the floor at all, not the way they did. It went along the diagonal, the one line nobody had treated as anything but a wall, and it went past every road and gate the five of them had built, the way a river in flood goes past a field's hedges.

She came out of the lane at the north-west end and took the north-west platform.

Ephram was on it, calling the next rotation, and he had barely begun when the lane put her at the top of his ramp. Her hand touched his shoulder. The platform was Auremont's, and what he was still saying was about a floor that had gone. He walked to his gate and put his hand on the post and walked back, and called again from behind the stack, at once and correctly, and by the time it reached anybody it was wrong again.

From the middle Cael could see quite clearly that there was nothing wrong with Ephram's calls. The floor they described simply kept ceasing to exist.

She went to Lira next.

Lira was at the north-east ramp. Half a beat early was Lira's whole trade. She had made a fighting life out of arriving first, and every arrival she had ever made had been timed against somebody's next step. The lane did not take steps. Lira read it coming. She went early, to the right place, with her one word in her mouth. And the lane was there before early. Daeva touched her on the back as she arrived, and was gone. Lira went to the gate and touched the post and came back, and did the right thing again, and it was the right thing again, and it was no use again.

Cael, watching from the middle, felt something he could only call pride.

She went past Brom.

That was the strangest of all of it. Brom was in his gap, the second one, where he had stood since the first call, and the lane went along the barrier's face right past him, four feet off, so close that the air of it pulled at his linen. It never came into his gap. It did not need to. It was not going through the barrier. It was going along it. Brom stood in his gate, and the road went by his gate without using it.

In the middle of the exchange Brom stepped out of the gap.

He did it of his own accord. Nobody called it. He looked at the lane going by, and at the gap he had held for two and a half exchanges, and he understood that the gap did not matter any longer, and he left it and went south to the platform in their own country to be of some use there. Cael had known Brom for a long time. He had never once seen him leave a place he had decided to hold. He thought it was brave, and that it cost Brom more than anything else on the floor.

She went to Karis.

Karis was in her frame at the north-west ramp, which was Auremont's again now, and had been made dear for nothing. Her frame priced the ways up to the platform, and the lane did not come up the ramp. It came down the length of the floor and off the end of the barrier and round, from nowhere a ramp was. Karis saw it come. She stood in her frame with her scorched hands open, and the touch landed on her arm, and she walked back to the gate.

Cael watched her the whole way. She did not look once at the frame she had planted and paid for twice and lost. She looked at the lane. She looked at all of it, the whole length of the barrier, both ends, as she walked, and her face had the stillness it had when she was reading a clause for the first time. She was taking notes without a notebook.

For a little more than a minute the squad stopped being a squad. It was five people standing in different parts of a floor, and she came to each of them in turn, like a caller working down a street.

We built a house on this floor, Cael thought, and there was only room in him for the one thought. She came in by a road it hasn't got a door for.

And then the lane turned toward him.

Afterward he could never decide if she had kept him till the end on purpose, or if he had simply been the last one she reached. He spent a whole page on it later and wrote at the bottom, honestly, Don't know.

He was in the middle, near the oak round, just south of the barrier's centre, where Ephram had sent him at the start of the exchange to watch both gaps. He felt the air begin to fold along the timber toward him, the long pressing weight that should not have been there, gathering. The crack of the lane's head. The flint smell.

The read went further than it had ever gone.

He could feel it going. All year it had read bodies, men's weight and direction half a beat early. All afternoon it had been reaching past them, for the heaviness along the wall that was not a body. Now, with the lane coming down the diagonal at him faster than he had ever seen anything move, he pushed it as far as it would go. It went into the air itself, into the place where the weight was pressed flat and about to snap back, and for the first time it read something that was not a person.

It gave him half a second.

Half a second of warning before the lane arrived. Against anybody else on the continent half a second would have bought him the whole exchange. Against her it bought him two steps.

He went sideways off his mark, two steps, not a burst, nothing on any sheet but feet. The lane came down the diagonal and resolved where he had been standing, on the stone beside the oak round, and spent itself there on nothing. The touch that had found three of the best fighters he knew, and passed the fourth by, found empty floor.

He was at the lane's edge, upright, inside the wash of it.

The air pushed at him. His ears popped. His hair stood up off his neck and arms, all of it, and the flint smell was so strong he could taste it. He was close enough to feel how much there was in the lane, how much more of it she was keeping on a leash, and he stood at the edge of it with his hands open and did not move.

And Daeva stopped.

Not for a beat. For one whole second, in the middle of the third exchange of a continental semifinal, with eight thousand people on their feet and roaring, she stopped. She stood at the mouth of the lane she had made, a stride from him, perfectly still.

She looked at him.

Her eyes went over him slowly. His feet first, and where his weight sat on them; then his open hands; then his shoulders; and last his face, where they stayed. He knew exactly what she was doing, because it was what he did himself, at every rail and every gate, to everybody, all day long. She was reading him.

Nobody ever had. In a year of wardens and evaluators and brass plates and panels, everybody who looked at him had been looking for a line to fill in or a figure to post. Nothing in her face was going to be written down anywhere. She meant to find out what he was before she went on, because he was on none of her tables.

Cael looked back. He did not know what she saw.

One second.

The roar came back into his ears all at once. She had turned away inside it, already moving, and the rest of the third exchange was hers by a long way.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

In the fourth exchange she let the lane go.

She came out of the east gate with the others and went back to being a piece on the board, quick and quiet and doing what she was sent to do. Whatever she had come to the third exchange to find out, she seemed to have found it.

And the five in plain colours did a thing almost nobody in the building understood.

They had been taken apart in front of the whole Concourse, one at a time, by something none of them had any answer for. Any squad in the trial's long history would have had every reason to come out for the fourth exchange broken.

They came out and put themselves back together.

Cael felt the read come back up to its ordinary depth and settle, and he began giving out the words again from the middle, and the others began answering them. Brom went back to the barrier, but not to his gap. He took a place two strides wide of it, where he could cover the gap and the barrier's face both, and priced the Silvers again from there. Karis planted her frame once more, at the north-east ramp, and planted it with a gap in it, a way through that she could close with one step, so that nothing coming from any direction could make the whole frame worthless at once. Lira stopped going early and began going ready, a little back, with her weight even, which cost her ground and saved her from being visited. And Ephram called, from the north-west ramp and then from behind the stack, in exactly the voice he had used in the first exchange, level and clear, counting aloud when he could not see.

It was not enough. It was close.

Once, near the end, Zerin came along the north rail at full speed on a flank run, and her line crossed Cael's in the middle. He saw her see him. She read him for two full beats, at a speed that should not have allowed anybody to read anything, and he saw her decide. She did not try him. She went round, wide, and spent her speed on Ephram's platform instead.

An economist, Cael thought, who won't buy what she can't price. He filed it. It was the first thing Auremont had ever written about him in real time, and it said: unknown cost, go round.

Auremont took the fourth exchange on the objective count by a few quarter-minutes.

The marshals' boards came up. The referee read them out.

Two exchanges to Halcenvane. Two to Auremont. And the trial, by the rules Rooke had read out once in the hired hall, went to the whole objective ledger. The third exchange alone had given Auremont more quarter-minutes than the first two had given Halcenvane together.

Auremont advanced to the final. Halcenvane would meet the other beaten semifinalist for third place.

The Concourse stood up.

It was not the cheer for a winner. Cael heard the difference at once. It was a long, deep, steady roar that went on and on, from every tier of the bowl, and every one of the eight thousand was on their feet for it, and it was for the house in plain colours that had lost. Every steward Cael spoke to afterward told him the same thing. The city stood like that for a beaten house perhaps twice in a cycle, and only when it had watched something it meant to remember.

Cael stood at the west gate with the other four and the Shield reserve, in the noise, and looked up at the bowl.

Somewhere along the north-tunnel wall, he knew, the exhibition frame still hung on its pegs, with the captain's line on it and the lake man's, and every line below them empty. After this afternoon, he thought, they would stay empty. There was nobody below Gold left in this city who would stand across a ring from him for the pleasure of finding out.

Two Silvers had filed. There would not be a third from anybody who still had a tier to lose.

Rooke stopped them in the tunnel.

It was half dark under the north tiers, and the roar of the bowl came down through the stone over their heads as a long dull thunder. He stood in their way with his coat over his arm and waited until all six of them, the five and the white-faced reserve, had stopped walking and were looking at him.

"Before anybody says a word to anybody," said Rooke. "The third exchange wasn't a squad problem."

Nobody said anything.

"I want that understood before you get to the stair, because by the stair you'll all have started blaming yourselves, and I won't have it." He looked from one of them to the next. "Nothing a squad does answers the third. Nothing a bracket fighter does, either. I've stood at a great many rails, and I've never once seen one fighter take a whole scenario floor away from nine others, and nobody else in this building has either. Every coach up there is writing that down right now in his own hand." He shifted the coat on his arm. "So nobody reviews it. Not you, and not me. The first two, and the fourth, we'll take apart tonight, and you'll be proud of every piece. The third goes in the file as weather."

He stood aside, and they went past him up the tunnel toward the light.

That night he did not hold a review at all, not in the way he usually held one. He passed his coaching sheet round the long table instead, face up, with a pencil, and told each of them to write one line on it, their own finding, and pass it on.

Lira wrote Ready. Not early. and passed it to Brom.

Brom took a long time over his. He wrote Left the gap. Should have left it sooner. and looked at it, and pushed the sheet on to Karis without a word.

Karis wrote A frame with a door in it, very small, and then, under that, She came from where no ramp was. Think about that. She gave it to Ephram.

Ephram wrote South. and nothing else, and went red, and passed it to Cael.

Cael held the pencil over the sheet for a while. Then he wrote: The diagonal. I had it on paper this morning and didn't know what it was. He gave the sheet back to Rooke.

Rooke read all five lines, slowly, at the head of the table. He did not say anything about any of them. He folded the sheet into the coaching file, and closed the file, and sat with his hand flat on the cover of it for a moment longer than he needed to.

"That'll do," he said. "That'll do very well. Eat something."

Ephram found him later in the courtyard, by the pump, where Cael had gone down to put his right hand under the cold water, though it no longer needed it.

Ephram did not say anything at first. He worked the pump handle for him, three long strokes, and stood back, and waited until Cael had dried his hand on his shirt.

"At Halcenvane," he said, "I told myself I was going to be careful how I remembered it. All of it. You, especially." He looked at the water running away across the cobbles. "I have been careful. I've watched you from the rail for a year, and I've waited for a floor where I'd see it for myself, whatever it is, with nobody telling me what I was looking at. Today I was on the floor." He looked up. "And she was ahead. She had the exchange, and the floor, and the whole bowl on its feet for her, and she gave up a whole second of it to stand there and look at you. Like we look at you. Like you look at everything."

Cael took the hand and shook it.

The third entry in Hesk's book went under the inventory and the line about tomorrow.

Team trial, semifinal. Two exchanges each, and the ledger to Auremont on the third. For two of the four, the five of us were the best squad in the building, and the marshals counted it, and it's in their book now with ours. Last night I wrote down what the tournament was for, and today it turned out to be true.

And the third exchange was hers.

She stopped mid-trial to read me. Gold Rank 3, nineteen years old, and the first person at this tournament whose attention feels like mine. Filed under: things that are going to happen whether I schedule them or not.

Half.

He was still looking at it when somebody knocked on the open door.

He waited. She made him.

"Then your storm."

Chapter 47 — The Empty Board

The morning after the trial came in grey, with a wet wind off the harbour, and the first thing on the long table at breakfast was the other semifinal.

Ephram had it. He had been down to the outer court before anybody else was awake, as he went down most mornings now, and he came up the stair with three broadsides under his arm and a loaf under the other and set them all on the table together, the bread on top.

He sat down. "Rhagen. We're fighting Rhagen."

Nobody had known for certain. The other semifinal had been fought on the far floor the same afternoon as theirs, and the five of them had been in the tunnel with Rooke and then at the long table with his review sheet, and by the time anybody thought to ask, the result had gone the rounds of the city without coming up their stair.

Karis pulled the top sheet out from under the loaf and read the column aloud, in the flat voice she used for things that were going to be argued about.

Rhagen had touched more people than the river academy had. It had touched a great many more; the flags had gone up for black-and-glass all afternoon. And the river academy had stood on two platforms out of three for most of every exchange, and let itself be touched, and gone to its gate and put its hand on the post and come back, and stood on them again.

"More touches, less ground." Karis put the sheet down. "And the ledger counts ground."

Lira snorted. "It's a good lesson. I'm glad somebody else had to pay for it."

Ephram was already buttering the loaf. "Twenty-first day, then, for third. Against the captain and Marek both, I should think, and whoever they've got who can carry a bag."

Brom had not said anything. He had a folded paper of his own beside his plate, and he waited until the others had finished with the broadsides before he unfolded it, because Brom read things at the table or not at all.

It was a single leaf, printed small, in the clean type of the commercial shops, and a printer in the delegation quarter had been selling it since before dawn for a copper to anybody who already owned the rest of the file, which by the length of the queue Ephram described was a good part of the city. It was meant to go in at the back. It had the shop's mark at the top and a date and a title, and under the title one line in italics.

Survived Daeva's lane at trial speed.

Under that the shop had added three paragraphs of what it called analysis. Brom did not read those aloud. He read the line twice, to himself, moving his lips a little, and then he passed the leaf to Cael across the bread.

"New last page," he said.

Cael read it. It was accurate, which was the trouble with the shops; they were nearly always accurate. They wrote down what had happened and left out what it meant, and anybody who bought the page could put the meaning back in for himself.

"It shuts the frame," said Karis.

She did not say it as if it were news. She said it as if she were checking a sum she had already done.

"Anybody below Gold who files against you now, files against that line," she went on. "Win, and he's beaten a boy who got out of the way of something. Lose, and he's the first man in the city to do worse against you than she did. There's no price on that trade anybody sensible will pay." She tapped the leaf. "They printed the end of the exhibitions and sold it for a copper."

"Then I'll have more time to train for Rhagen."

He meant it as a joke, more or less, and Lira laughed, more or less. But Brom took the leaf back and folded it along its crease and put it in his coat with the rest of the file, and nobody else at the table laughed at all.

The exhibition frame hung where it had hung all sitting, on its pegs at the mouth of the north tunnel, under an old lamp-bracket that nobody lit any more.

After breakfast Cael's feet took him past it. He told himself it was on the way to the hired hall, which it nearly was.

It was dark wood, older than anything around it, with the type of a printer who had been dead for a very long time. Five short lines of rule ran across the top of it. Below them the ring's size and the rating provision, and then the ruled lines, a long column of them, waiting. Two were filled. The Rhagen captain's name was on the first, in a clerk's careful white, and the lake man's on the second. Below the lake man the lines went on down the board, empty, to the bottom of the frame.

Beside it, in a glass case on an iron stand, lay the register.

Every morning at the first bell a steward opened it. He was a narrow, tidy man with a bunch of keys on a cord round his wrist, one of the west tower's outer staff. Cael had seen him before, on the mornings of the two Silver filings, and he had had the look then of somebody who had expected the easiest posting in the building and had been mildly put out to find it wasn't. He unlocked the case. He opened the register at its ribbon and read down the page to the last entry, and looked up at the frame, and checked one against the other. Then he shut the book and locked the case and stepped back to the wall and stood there, with his hands behind him, for the hour the rules required.

There were about thirty people watching him do it. Some had come on purpose. Some had stopped on their way through the tunnel and stayed. Nobody said anything. When the hour was up the steward took his keys and went, and the thirty went too, slowly, as people leave a quay when the ship they were waiting for has not come in.

Cael stood a moment longer, looking at the empty lines.

He had told himself, the night before, that they would stay empty, and he found that he did not much like being right. He went on to the hired hall with the frame still in front of his eyes, and was late, and Rooke said nothing about it, which was worse.

Rooke had them there by the second bell, with the door shut and his coaching sheet open on the trestle at the page with the five lines on it.

"Rhagen. Four mornings from now. They'll bring the captain and Marek both. They'll bring their structure, which is the best structure on this continent. And they'll have spent last night doing to our semifinal what we did to theirs." He put his finger on the sheet. "So we'll take our own medicine first. One line each. You wrote them. He began with Lira.

Ready. Not early. She had written it herself, and she knew exactly what it cost. Early had been her whole trade since she was small: arrive first, take the corner, make the other fighter's next step land in a place she already owned. Ready was a different thing. Ready was a little further back, with the weight even, waiting for the floor to tell her where to go instead of telling the floor.

He set her against the Stone reserve in a chalk corner and made her stand off it. Twice she went early anyway, out of pure habit, and the reserve went round her.

"Again. Early is a guess you make for the other man. Ready lets him make it."

The third time she stood, and waited, and went when the reserve went, half a beat behind his start and a stride ahead of his arrival, and took the corner off him without a burst.

"That," said Rooke.

Brom was next. Left the gap. Should have left it sooner. Rooke did not make him stand in a gap at all. He chalked one on the floor between two benches and put Brom two strides wide of it, off to one side, where he could reach the mouth of it in a single step and still see past it.

Rooke tapped the chalk with his boot. "A gap with a man in it is a wall. Everybody can see a wall. A gap with a man beside it is a gap. It looks like a way through. Let it look like one."

Brom considered the chalk, with his bandaged arms folded.

"So I'm a toll," he said. "Not a door."

Karis had her frame. A frame with a door in it. She planted her three anchors on the boards in the order Ternhall had taught her, leading foot, a stride forward on the line, the flank, and then she took the flank anchor out and moved it half a stride, so that the frame stood with one side open. The opening was real. Anybody could have walked through it. But she could close it with one step, and only she knew which step.

The story of the Silver reached the long table at supper that night, the way stories reached it, by way of Ephram.

A Silver from one of the eastern houses had come down to the frame that afternoon, long after the register's hour. He was a Five, a big quiet man who had gone out of his bracket in the round of sixteen and had nothing left at the sitting but his number. He had walked up to it with a filing form in his hand, filled in, to be ready for the morning. Half the tunnel had seen it.

He had stood in front of the frame for a long time. He had read the captain's line, and the lake man's, and the two figures posted beside them. Then he had read the empty line underneath, the one his own name would have gone on.

Then he had folded his form in half and put it back inside his coat, and buttoned the coat over it, and gone away down the tunnel.

"Nobody entered anything," Ephram went on. "A form you don't hand in isn't a form. So officially it never happened. But I had it from three people, and they all said the same thing about him, which was that he didn't look frightened. He looked like a man adding up."

"It was by the time it got to me." And the table laughed, which was the first time it had laughed properly since the tunnel.

On the second morning it rained.

It was not hard rain. It was the soft, steady, salt-smelling kind that Norhold seemed to keep for days when it had nothing else planned, and it came in under the tunnel's arch and lay in a skin on the stone. At the first bell the steward arrived with his keys, as always. He walked out of the tunnel's dry part into the wet part, where the frame was, and stopped.

There were two hundred people waiting for him.

Cael counted them, because counting was what he did when he did not know what to feel. They stood in the rain in a loose half-ring round the case, in coats and hoods and under borrowed sacking, with the water running off their hat-brims. There were dockhands, and two ladies with an umbrella between them, and a boy on his father's shoulders, and a knot of students in somebody's yellow. None of them was a fighter. None of them had anything to file. They had come to watch a man unlock a glass case and read a book.

The steward did it exactly as he had done it the day before.

He did not hurry, and he did not look up at the crowd, not once. He unlocked the case and opened the book and read the last entry and looked at the frame and checked one against the other, with the rain darkening the shoulders of his coat, and shut the book and locked the case and went and stood against the wall with his hands behind his back. When the hour was over he took his keys and left. Cael thought it was a fine piece of ordinary work, and he wrote it down that night in the old volume's last leaves, in four words, because the old volume was running out.

The broadsides had found the frame by then. They ran it on every front sheet in the outer court, in the largest type any of them owned.

WHO FIGHTS THE ENROLLEE?

Under the awnings the betting rows, which had refused all sitting to take money on his bouts, had found a way round their own sign. They would not book a bout that had not been filed. But they would book whether one would be. By the middle of the morning there was a price chalked on four boards on no further filing at this sitting, and it was getting shorter every hour.

He bought a twist of hot bread at a stall on the basin steps and stood under the stall's canvas to eat it, because the rain had come on harder.

Two wharfmen and a woman from the fish market were arguing at the counter. They had a broadside spread on the planks between them, held down at the corners with a weight and a knife and two cups. None of them had any money on the exhibitions, because nobody did. None of them had looked twice at the boy in the plain coat eating bread behind them. They were simply doing what the whole city was doing that morning, which was working it out.

"It's his own fault for being good," said one of the wharfmen. "Nobody wants to be the man he beats."

The other shook his head. "Nobody wants to be the man he doesn't beat, either. Look at the Silvers. They lost and they're heroes. Who files to be the third hero? It's the same bout twice."

The fishwife had been gutting a fish while they talked, and she finished it and laid it down on the paper, which neither wharfman thought much of.

"You're both looking at it from underneath," she said. "Nobody's going up to him any more. Fine. He's too high to climb to." She wiped her knife. "So somebody's got to come down."

The wharfmen looked at her.

"That's all," she said, and picked up the next fish.

Cael finished his bread, and thanked the stall-keeper, and went out into the rain. He found he was smiling, and he was not altogether sure why, and by the time he reached the hired hall he had stopped.

"Off something. I don't know what."

"Then let's find out what." She was already pulling off her coat. "Shut your eyes."

The hired hall was a long room with boarded walls and a stack of barrels down one side, and Karis had taken the bench by the window with her notebook, and Brom had gone to the door to keep it. Cael stood in the middle of the floor with his eyes shut. Lira went to the far end.

"I'll come past you. One burst. I won't say when. You tell me when it gets to you."

He stood and listened, and heard her feet settle on the boards forty feet away. He reached for her with the read, the way he reached for everybody, and found her at once: her weight, low and even, the small gathering of it into the leading hip that came before every burst she had ever made.

"Now," he said.

She went. The burst carried her the length of the hall and past him on his left, a pace off, and her wash went over him a moment later, a push of air on his cheek and his ear and his shirt.

"You called me," came Lira's voice from the other end. "Not it."

He knew. He had called her start, which he had been able to call for years. The push had arrived after, a long way after, at a time the read had not told him anything about at all.

They did it again. Twelve times. Every time he caught the gathering in her hip and every time he called it, because he could not help calling it; it was the loudest thing in the room. And every time the wash came over him late, on its own clock, and he had no idea it was coming until it came.

On the twelfth, Karis spoke from the window. "You're reading her. You're very good at reading her. Read what she leaves behind."

"I don't know how."

"I know you don't." Karis wrote something down. "That's why I said it."

He opened his eyes. Lira was leaning on the barrels at the far end with her hands on her knees, grinning, not much out of breath.

"Your storm is going to take longer than an afternoon."

Karis said the rest of it at supper that night, because somebody had to.

"Two days."

She had the frame drawn in the back of her notebook, from memory, with its two filled lines and its column of empty ones. She had been watching it the way she watched any instrument she had predicted, waiting to see whether it would do what she said.

"It's done what I said. It can't fill from below. Everybody underneath him has priced himself out." She closed the notebook. "So it fills from above, or it dies."

Nobody said what was above.

There was exactly one name above, and every one of them had been not saying it since the tunnel. It had become a kind of rule among them without anybody making it, the way the long table's rules got made: the name was not to be spent before its time. Brom ate his supper. Ephram looked at his plate. Lira, who left nothing unsaid that she wanted said, put her cup down and looked across at Cael and said nothing at all.

He went up early. He did not sleep early.

He lay in the dark under the window with the rain on the glass, and thought about the frame on its pegs in the tunnel with the water running past it, and the steward's keys, and the man who had put his form back in his coat. He thought about the fishwife. Somebody's got to come down.

He thought about one second, at the mouth of a lane, with the air pushing at him and his hair standing up off his neck, and a woman a stride away looking at his feet and his hands and his face.

Then he made himself stop thinking about it, which took some time, and slept.

Chapter 48 — Overdue

On the third morning Cael was in the warm-up hall under the east tower at the first bell, working evasions with Brom on the far mat, and he heard it before anybody told him.

It was an ordinary morning, as far as it went. The hip had held through two days of work without a murmur. The burn on his right hand had gone from pink to a pale shine he could only find if he looked for it. Brom stood in the middle of the mat with his bandaged forearms up and came at him at three-quarter pace, a heavy man's walk with a shove at the end of it, and Cael went round the shove, left and then right and then left again, on his feet, no bursts, as Rooke wanted it two days before a trial.

The hall had its own noise at that hour, and he knew it by now as well as he knew the noise of the long table. It was wide and busy. Thirty conversations, none of them about anything. Feet on mats. Somebody's coach counting. A crew somewhere down the far end of the building knocking wedges into something with a mallet.

The coach was the first thing to go.

He had been counting a Blade through a drill two mats away, four, five, six, and at seven he simply stopped, with his mouth still open on the next number. Then the mallet at the far end stopped, between one wedge and the next. Cael did not hear anything begin. He heard things end, one after another, as if somebody were walking through the building pinching out candles. Thirty conversations became twenty, became ten, became one conversation said thirty times, and all thirty were turned the same way, toward the courtyard doors and whatever was on the other side of them.

Brom lowered his hands. He did not look at the doors. He looked at Cael.

"That's a filing," he said.

The Blade two mats over was already walking toward the doors with his practice lath still in his fist, and his coach was walking after him, and neither of them had said a word to the other.

Seln came in by the east door a little after that. He came at his usual pace, which was the pace of a man going to fetch a ledger from a shelf, through a building in which a great many other people had begun to walk quickly. He had a single sheet in his hand, the adjudication office's copy with its seal still on it, and he did not hurry and did not look at anybody, and the people near the door moved aside for him without knowing why.

He stopped at the rail of the third mat and held the sheet out.

"The office's copy," he said. "Posted at the first bell. I thought you would prefer to read it before you heard it read."

Cael took it.

It was the category's own form, the plain printed one, with the boxes in the same order as the two Silver filings had used. The name was in the first box, in a clear upright hand that had not hurried. The house was in the second. In the box for tier, where the season's two volunteers had written Silver, she had written Gold, and the rank beside it, Three.

At the foot of the form was the box the category gave a challenger to state a reason. The captain had filled his with two words. The lake man had filled his with two. She had filled hers with one.

Overdue.

Cael read it twice. Then he handed it to Brom, who read it once and handed it back, and the three of them stood at the rail of the third mat while the warm-up hall emptied around them toward the outer court.

Things that are going to happen whether I schedule them or not. He had written that three nights ago, in Hesk's book, under the trial. He had thought then that he was being dry.

"Mm," said Seln, and went away to find Rooke.

The city did not take the news in one piece. It took it in every way it had, all at once, and it spent the day finding out how many ways that was.

The criers had it within the hour. The broadsides had a sheet out by the third bell with the form reprinted on it, box by box, and the one word in the last box printed in type an inch high. By noon Cael had seen it chalked on a wall, painted on a cooper's board, and cut into the crust of a pie in a cookshop window by somebody with a steady knife. The betting rows wiped the price on no further filing off all four boards at once and did not put up anything in its place.

Bracken brought the west tower's half of it to the long table at midday, with the pouch under his arm and the expression of a man who has been given a very good piece of gossip by a colleague and intends to hand it on with every courtesy.

"The office," he said, sitting down, "is in difficulties."

He took a piece of bread. He had begun doing that at their table, and nobody remarked on it.

"There are three of them," he said, "and the Chief Adjudicator's people are working on all three at once, which I'm told is not their custom. The first is precedent. There isn't one. They've had the category's papers up from the strong room, all three hundred years of them, and a clerk I know spent the morning reading through every filing ever made under it. Copper against Copper. Copper against Iron, a few. A Silver once, in a cycle nobody living remembers, against a man who withdrew." He buttered the bread. "Nothing above Silver, ever. Nothing against a practitioner with no tier at all, except the two this sitting. They have an archive, and it's empty in the shape of this."

"And the second?" said Karis, who had a pencil out.

"Insurance." Bracken almost smiled. "The tournament's underwriters price every bout on the difference between the two tiers. They have a printed schedule with a row for every difference anybody ever imagined. There is no row for this one, because this one isn't a difference. The counsel has been sitting with the underwriters' man since the second bell. My colleague says he went in with a clean collar."

Lira laughed into her cup.

"And the third," said Bracken, and the almost-smile went away, "is the one that matters. A demonstration bout is rated. It must be. That's what the provision is for. The Standard's tables run from the bottom of Copper to the best recorded Gold, and every figure on them is worked out from where the two fighters stand on the scale against each other." He laid the knife down. "One of these two doesn't stand on the scale. The tables would be asked to divide a performance by an empty space. My colleague's word for it was a division by a blank, and he didn't say it as a joke."

Nobody at the table said it as one either.

The other half of the day came by the outer court, where everything came in the end.

Auremont had objected. It had done it in writing, in the morning, through its delegation head, to the adjudication office and to the girl both: the risk, the insurers, the finals calendar, the program's duty to its practitioner. A copy had been posted, because the category posted everything. It was a careful document, and a long one, and it had the look of a thing written by honest people in a hurry who knew what it was for.

She had not answered it.

Lira read the posted copy over a stranger's shoulder in the outer court and came back to the long table looking thoughtful.

"They're not fighting her," she said. "They can't. Karis, tell me I'm right."

"You're right." Karis did not even look up. "There's nothing in the charter that lets a house take back what one of its own has signed. They know it. That paper isn't meant to stop her. It's meant to be found in a drawer in ten years, so that everybody can see Auremont said no."

"And she just went to her afternoon session," said Lira, half to herself. "As if it were weather."

The broadsides had noticed the same thing, and they were gentle about it, gentler than Cael would have guessed. The best of them, a sheet from the harbour end that usually cared for nothing but odds, gave her a whole column without a single price in it. For seven years, it said, a great house has told the finest fighter of her age where to stand, and she has stood there, and stood there beautifully. This morning she chose a floor for herself. We do not know what she will find on it. Neither, we suspect, does she. That is the first thing about her this paper has ever been unable to quote odds on, and we find we do not mind.

The office hung it at dusk. The five of them went down to read it after supper, because nobody in Norhold read a draw alone, and this was as near to a draw as made no difference.
