Nobody made a sound.

Ephram told him afterwards how it had gone outside. He had gone round the cookshops and the quay steps that night with his ruined voice, asking, and come back with it in order, and the part he wanted Cael to have was one moment in the outer court. The people who could not get in had been following the bout from a man on a barrel at the mouth of the east tunnel, who could see a slice of the floor and called it out to them, exchange by exchange, as a crier calls a race. He called the lane. He got as far as and the boy — and stopped, with his mouth still open and the whole court looking up at him, for ten seconds by a carter's count. Under the awnings behind him, in the same ten seconds, the betting men, who had a price chalked for every half point of the Standard and none for this, turned their ledgers over on the boards one after another, face down, without a word, and stood with their hands on them. Then the court shouted at the man on the barrel to go on, and he said he was sorry. He had run out of sentence.

On the tower stairs a woman near the top asked the man in front of her what had happened, and forty people on the steps below answered her at once, in four different accents, with the same three words in four different orders. Every version came out meaning he hasn't got that.

He had a breath to see it. Then the cost came due.

He had always paid it later. After every one of the others there had been a quiet room and a day or two, and in that time everything in him had shifted a little, unhurried, to make room. This one would not wait for a room. It came now, on the stone, with a Gold still in the exchange, and it came all at once. The new thing was heavier than anything he had ever carried, and the moment it was in him everything else in him turned toward it, the way every head in a hall turns when a door bangs.

He went to step toward her. The exchange was not over.

He called for the landing beat, and the wrong thing answered.

It was like calling a dog by its name in a yard full of dogs. He had called the Wind as he had called it every day for years, without thinking, and something else lifted its head instead. It was the new thing, raw and enormous and not yet sure where it lived, answering to a name that was not its own. The Wind did not come at all. The foot came down on the stone with nothing behind it. Nothing was wrong with the stone. The man with the level had set it true, and it was true still. It was the leg that had been given the wrong instruction, by the wrong part of him.

It did not hurt. That was the frightening part. It was a question of ownership. For years every one of the things he carried had come when he called it, with no gap at all between the calling and the coming, as a hand comes. Now he did not know which of them was his to call. He stood for an instant in the middle of himself like a man in his own house who has put his hand out for the door in the dark and found a wall.

He stumbled.

The bowl saw it. They had seen him go through the air and come out the other side of it, and now, half a breath later, they saw him fail to take an ordinary step on an ordinary floor. He heard them see it. It was a low sound, like a crowd on a quay watching a man go into the water.

It frightened him, and he let it, because there was no time to do anything else. And then the thing Brom had been putting into him all year, a little at a time, every time he went down on the boards, came up of its own accord. Chin in. Arms in. Loose. Nothing left lying out. He went down the way he had been taught to go down. He had not known he had learned it.

She was a pace away, and he was falling at her feet with the left side open and nothing left in his legs.

He saw the choice reach her. He saw it as plainly as he had ever seen a weight move in a fighter's hips. A touch on him now would level the flags. A fire into him now would finish the bout in a way the woodcutters on the quays could have sold for the rest of their lives: the Gold over the fallen boy, with the storm round her head. It was lying on the floor for her. It would have cost her nothing at all.

She did not lay a lane. She did not lift a hand.

Something happened to the air under him.

He felt it as he fell, and from where he was it felt like the air thickening. It was like falling into a bale of wool. Something took hold of all of him at once, gently, and slowed him, so that he did not hit the stone at all; he arrived on it. He came down onto one knee and the heel of one hand, as quietly as a man kneeling in a chapel. Then the air let go of him and was air again.

She stepped back a pace. She let her hands hang open at her sides, where everybody could see them. Then she turned her head and looked at the referee.

The referee looked at her, and at him, kneeling. He crossed his arms high over his head.

"Stoppage."

At the long table on the west side the Chief Adjudicator was already on his feet. He did not raise his voice. In that bowl, just then, he would only have had to whisper.

"Stoppage. Daeva."

After that the tournament did what it had done for three hundred years, slowly, in its own order, and Cael watched all of it from one knee. Watching was the one part of him still working the way it always had.

The referee kept his arms crossed above his head until each of them had nodded to him. Whoever had written the protocols had once watched a healer run across a floor in front of a crowd, he thought, and had never wanted to see it again.

He could see what it was costing them to stay up there. He put it away carefully, for the book, beside everything else. Five people not running to him. He thought it was probably the hardest thing any of them had done all day.

He was still on one knee when it came.

It arrived where it always arrived, in the place behind his eyes that belonged to nothing else, with no interest at all in where he was or who was looking. It had come to him in a yard and on a stair and in a shut room at Halcenvane. It came to him now on the stone of a bowl with eight thousand people in it, and the healer's two fingers in his left hand, and not one of the eight thousand could see it but him.

He read it through twice, and then, because he could not help it, he counted.

She came back across the floor.

Her own people were calling her from the south break. She lifted one hand behind her without turning round, and they stopped. She came across the stone at an ordinary walking pace and stood over him, and held out her hand. It was not the hand fighters give each other after a bout, and it was not a coach's hand either. She held it out low and open, palm up, as you might hold out a hand to someone sitting on a step.

He took it. She drew him up onto his feet, and laid her other palm against his left side for a moment, not asking, to keep him steady, and then took it away as if it had not been there.

"That was mine," she said.

She said it for the two of them, under the noise that was beginning to come back into the bowl. She did not sound angry, or as if she were asking. She set it down between them like a figure read off a board. Then she waited.

"A piece of it," said Cael.

It was the truest thing he could give her without giving her the rest, and the rest was not his alone to give. It belonged to four people and a book. But the shape of it she had bought. Nobody else had ever bought anything off him that way. She had stood in front of a full bowl and come at him with all she had, and that was the price.

She went on looking at him. He watched something rise in her face, from a long way down, the way a swimmer comes up out of deep water into light. It was delight, plain and whole.

"Nineteen years," she said. "Nobody has ever shown me something I couldn't name."

Then the healers closed round them, and two officials, and a pair of stewards with a stretcher. She told the stretcher to go away before he could. As the ring of people tightened she leaned in between two of them and spoke once more, low, as if she were setting a time and a place.

"Find out what you are. Then find me. I want the rematch with whatever that is."

She went back across the stone to her own gate, and did not look round.

At the north rail Rooke had taken his hand back. He said something to the air, but the younger healer heard it and said it again at her own supper table that night, and by the end of the week it had reached the bluff by three roads. It was the version the house kept.

"That's the whole education, right there. Not the lane. The mercy, on a clock."

Cael looked up once more, past the officials, to the high row over the east rail. Every face in it was turned down toward the floor. Every face but one. The man in plain grey at the end of the row was standing, and going along behind the plated chairs toward the east stair, at the same unhurried pace he had used on the day of the duelist.

Before the figure, Cael thought. Again.

Then the healers turned him toward his own gate, and he let them.

The healer in Auremont's warm-up room found the mark on the third look.

It was on the front of Daeva's left shoulder, a little below the collarbone, where his palm had been. A round red place the size of a coin, with the skin shining at its middle. It was not a burn worth the name. The healer, who had been with the program since before Daeva came to it, dabbed salve on it with the tip of one finger and then stood back and looked at it for a long while, as if it were a word written on a wall in a hand she did not know.

"Four years," the healer said at last.

Daeva said nothing. She had been counting too.

She sat on the bench under the room's one lamp with her shirt off the shoulder and her hands in her lap and let them all come and go. The room was full of her house. Her lead instructor stood in the doorway with his hands behind his back, tipping his head at her and not saying anything, which was the kindest thing he could have done. The delegation head came in, and said that the house was very proud, in a voice that did not know what it was proud of, and went out again. Two of the design staff stood by the far wall arguing in whispers over a chart that had nothing on it yet.

The risk officer came last, with the folded sheet in his hand that the foreman had carried all night in his coat and taken out and read before every bolt went in, and that had held. He did not sit down. He stood in front of her and opened the sheet and closed it again.

"The north mast took it," he said. "All of it. The trench carried it east, the way it falls. Nothing went into the rows." He looked at the sheet as if he had never seen it before. "I worked that sheet out against you. Every line of it was you. I didn't know what to work out for him, so I didn't." He folded it smaller. "It held anyway."

"It was a good sheet," said Daeva.

He nodded several times, and went out with it, and she heard him on the stair saying something to somebody about the cable, and then nothing.

When they had all gone she sat on alone with the salve drying on her shoulder, and thought about the lane.

It had been hers. She had known it the moment it opened, before her mind had caught up, the way you know your own name called across a street before you have turned round. Nobody else on the continent laid a lane like that. She had watched the coast Storms, and the old border Golds, and the one man from the eastern islands who came every cycle and lost in the second round. Their lanes were theirs, each one, the way a voice is somebody's. This one had been hers. It had been small and rough and laid crosswise out of a corner, where she would never have laid it, by somebody who had plainly never laid one before. But it had her grain in it. It had the little hitch at its far end where she always asked the air hardest. It was like hearing a bar of a tune she had made up as a child, whistled back to her by a stranger in the street. It was in the wrong key, and too short, but hers.

She did not try to work out how he had done it.

She noticed that she did not try, and she was glad, as she had been glad six days ago on the floor of the boarded room. People had spent her whole life working out how she did things. They had built rooms and programs and floors for it, and written it all down, and every word they wrote had been true, and none of them had ever once got near her. She was not going to do that to him. She would not have known where to start anyway. She only knew that it was hers, and that it had come out of him, and that she had never in her life been so happy about anything she did not understand.

Then she thought about the end.

He had been going down at her feet with his side open and his legs gone, and she had seen the finish lying there, and she had not taken it. She had not decided not to, exactly. She had done what her hands knew. She had let the air under him go slack, so that it would not hold him up and would not let him fall either, but take him down slow, like a hand lowering a cup to a table. From her side it was a letting go. She had stopped asking anything at all of the air under him, and let it lie. To him, she supposed, falling into that, it would have felt the other way about, like being caught in water.

It was the thing the big quiet man had done to her on the coast when she was fifteen. She had spent a month of mornings learning never to let anybody do it to her again, and she had kept the exercise sheet ever since because it was the only honest record of a thing that had been done to her. She had always thought of it as the thing that had beaten her once.

It had not occurred to her before this afternoon that a man might do it to catch somebody.

That kept her on the bench until the lamp needed trimming. She thought perhaps he had not meant it kindly, the big quiet man, all those years ago. Perhaps he had. It did not much matter now. What mattered was that there were two ways to use it, and she had only ever been shown one.

That night, in the marbled notebook in the lining of her case, she wrote one line under all the others. She wrote it slowly, in her best hand, and read it twice, and put the book away.

Today somebody asked me something.

The junior clerk had gone down for the stamp, and Umber stood at the window and waited for him to come back.

It was the only thing left to wait for. The sheet lay on the black table behind him with nine names at its foot, the ink of the last one still wet. At the first bell after midnight he had made her try.

That had been his rule from the start of the sitting, and he had said it before anybody else could speak. Nobody would argue about what to do in that room until the room had done the ordinary thing, aloud, start to finish, with the clerks writing down every step. He remembered her finger going down the index, down one page and then over and down the next. There was nothing under Storm for a fighter with no Storm in his record. The guesses came up the stair with every visitor, all day, and he wrote every one of them down.

The betting men believed that one, he said. Any fighter of good discipline might do a thing like that at that size, the man said, and the continent had simply never seen one try. He had not been in the building.

And on the second morning there was the sixth. It came from the fishwife at the end of the quay, who had it from her sister, who sold to Auremont's kitchen. Daeva had done it. That was the only one he copied into the book with any respect. It was the only guess on the continent that had started from a true thing. The lane had been hers. And from there it had set off in the one wrong direction there was, and gone farther along it than he would have believed anybody could.

The city argued about it all that day. Then Auremont ended it. Its coaching staff sent four words to all four broadsides at once, unasked, and every one of them printed the words the next morning in the largest type they had.

our fighter does not mis-seed.

He wrote all six into Hesk's book that night, one under another, and drew a line beneath them, and wrote under the line.

Six guesses from a city that has argued about fighters for three hundred years. Every one of them reaches for a shape the world already owns: a secret register, a hidden Path, a cheat, a slip. Not one comes near. What happened doesn't have a shape in anybody's head yet, and you can't guess at a thing you can't picture. Nobody guesses digestion. I'd thought what kept it hidden was us, the four of us and this book. It isn't. It's that nobody can imagine it.

Chapter 58 — The Weather

[Firm, lucid narration; build through the final standard and let the aftermath breathe]

The file reached Ilsev's desk a little before noon, in the observation office's own case, with the west tower's seal on its cord.

She had known it would come. The entry's last word was Referred, and the charter gave only one address for a thing shown on a floor outside classification, which was the Compact's observation seat at the tournament. That was her. So she had come up to the office early and cleared the desk and laid out a fresh sheet of the office's paper, and when the case came she cut the cord and took the papers out in order and laid them in a row: the match record; the nine charts, in copy; the scribes' three accounts; the healers' report from the north station; and on top of all of them, by itself, the entry.

She read the entry first, once, as she read everything. She read it a second time for the words alone, as she had been taught to do, long ago, by a woman who read a form the way a jeweller looks at a stone. Under, not by. She noted that. Somebody had been careful, at the end of a long night.

Then she began on the routing, which was her work and had been her work since before most of the clerks in the building were born: a minute on the front sheet to say what the file was and whom it went to next, and why, and under what article. She knew the article without looking. She wrote it in her small upright hand and blotted it, and reached into the case for the dispatch slip that would send it on up the line.

There was a second packet under the dispatch slip.

It had come in the same case, by the same courier, from a different office altogether. Her own name was on it in a clerk's hand, and she knew the shape of it before she opened it.

The designation in the enrollee's file had been her question for a long while. She had first sent it up from Greyvane, plainly, asking who had entered the mark and on whose authority. Twice it had come back down to her with the same two sentences, no originating authority of record, and the second time a third sentence latched on behind them, saying the same nothing more firmly. So last year at Halcenvane, on the fifteenth of Reaping, she had sat at the long table in the emptied hall and filled in a second referral, fuller, every date and reference in its order, and marked it a level higher than the office that had answered. In all her years she had never before filed twice on one matter. A question nobody answered was a question to be asked again, through the next door up.

This was that door's answer.

She slit the packet and took out the return. It was one line, in a registry clerk's round hand, with a stamp she did not know.

Referral closed at registry level; no further inquiry authorized.

She sat and looked at it.

Every reader of records learns early that the registry can say no in a hundred ways. Not of record. Not found. No file. The registry was full of honest holes, places where something had once been written down and later lost, or never written down at all. She had filed hundreds of those holes in her time without losing a night's sleep over any of them. A hole was only a hole. You marked it, and went round it.

This was not a hole. A hole said, there is nothing here. This said, there is something here, and you may not look at it. It did not say who had decided that. There was no name under the stamp. There was no office she could write to and ask. It was a drawer somebody had nailed shut and then taken the hammer away.

And it had come to her desk in the same case as a file from the west tower asking the Compact to look closely at the same boy.

She laid the two sheets side by side on the desk. The entry, which asked her to inquire. The return, which forbade it. She looked from one to the other for some time.

Then she did a thing she had not done once in her working life.

She opened the bottom drawer of the desk, where she kept her own things, and took out a sheet of paper that was not the office's. It was a sheet she had bought for herself at a stationer's on the coopers' row on her second day in the city, for letters home, and never used. She laid it on top of everything else, over the office's paper, and she wrote on it. She did not write in her office hand. She wrote in the hand she had used as a girl at her mother's table, before anybody had taught her to make her letters stand up straight.

What she wrote, nobody ever read, because it was not for any file and not addressed to anybody, and it was the first thing she had written in all her years of service that was not meant to be read by somebody else. She wrote it, and read it through once, and folded it twice, and put it inside her coat, against her chest, where she had never in her life carried anything that belonged to the Compact.

Then she finished the routing minute on the front sheet, correctly, under the right article, and sent the file on up the line as the charter required.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Havel brought the second round of the dispatch case in at the half after noon, and saw only the paper.

It was not office stock; he knew office stock as he knew his own boots. He saw her fold it twice and put it inside her coat, and pick up her office pen again. He did not look for the words. He did not need to. He had four sheets of his own like it, carried through three postings and now in his kit between the second and third of his manuals, where nobody ever looked.

That night, in his narrow room at the inn behind the east tower, he wrote a fifth. At its head he put the line from the return, which he had read upside down on her desk in perhaps three seconds and found he had entire.

Referral closed at registry level; no further inquiry authorized.

Under it he wrote that the senior seat now kept a sheet of its own. Then he put the fifth in with the other four between the manuals and buckled the kit, and sat for a while in the dark, thinking that there were two of them now in one city, each with papers their office had not asked for, and neither going to tell the other.
